articles.title: Raffy Tulfo flags expired medicines, P556M Tala warehouse delays
articles.summary: Senator Raffy Tulfo slammed the Department of Health (DOH) for wasting medicine, citing a P13 million delivery worth of supplies that remained unused. He also flagged the slow construction of a…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 10:00pm
Senator Raffy Tulfo slammed the Department of Health (DOH) for wasting medicine, citing a P13 million delivery worth of supplies that remained unused.
He also flagged the slow construction of a warehouse in Caloocan City despite the half-billion spent on the project.

Before he began his presentation, Tulfo made a disclaimer that the present DOH administration, led by Secretary Edwin Mercado, was not the subject of his report, as the incidents occurred before his term. He presented a video showing the Tala hub warehouse in Caloocan City that was allegedly filled with expired medicine, with footage that was dated November 19.
Tulfo’s team allegedly uncovered 16 million syringes, which were reportedly from 2022 and were going to expire by October 2027.
The senator has previously accused the DOH of hiding or burying expired medicine.

“I obtained documents showing delivery of approximately P13 million worth of expired medicines and nutrition supplies to Tala Warehouse. But I’m not convinced that the alleged burial involved only P13 million.” Tulfo said.

Tulfo said that there were also nutrition packs being bought but allowed to expire, year after year. The senator asked if it would be better to delegate the task to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
He added that the matter should also be investigated by the Office of the Ombudsman.
Senator JV Ejercito, the DOH’s budget sponsor, said that the agency was already coordinating with the DSWD for the nutrition packs, which were focused on the first 1,000 days of babies.

“With regards po doon sa expired medicine issue, they have consolidated offices to ensure an end-to-end procurement and supply chain/ Ito po yung ginawa nila through digitalization para ma-monitor nila yung supplies and dedicated staffing for this purpose para magkaroon ng better forecasting in procurement para hindi na po masayang itong gamit,” Ejercito said.

(With regard to the expired medicine issue, they have consolidated offices to ensure an end-to-end procurement and supply chain. They are doing it through digitalization so that they can monitor the supplies and have dedicated staffing for this purpose, so that there is better forecasting in procurement so that these supplies would not be wasted.)

Ejercito said that they have shifted to PhilHealth for the Gamot program so that the DOH does not keep procuring this way. The agency also assembled a team to probe the matter and said that they will submit an investigation report to Tulfo.

Tulfo raised other matters, such as the construction of the Tala warehouse. It received P90 million in funding for construction in the 2019 budget, and continued to receive money in 2021, 2022, and 2024. The budget allotted for the construction of the Tala warehouse amounted to P556.2 million.
Despite construction spanning seven years, Tulfo said that it was only 38% complete.
“They have a fund… meron pong budget ito na P510 million but they are in the process of re-bidding, and DOH intends to complete this by 2028,” Ejercito said.

Tulfo replied that this was too expensive for a warehouse, as taken together with what was already spent, it was more than P1 billion. Ejercito responded by saying that the DOH has already contracted a third-party quantity surveyor so that there is a new, accurate estimate for the completion of the project. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say
articles.summary: Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to lease treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’

blocks.text: Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.
The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.
Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne Law School, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.
“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.
“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster”, with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators.
Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”
Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.
Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.
“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.
“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”
Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.
O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.
“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.
A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”
“We are not selling Melbourne Water. It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.
“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”
The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.
The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

articles.title: Labor faces prospect of electoral wipeout in Victoria as voters turn to Liberals and One Nation
articles.summary: Former ALP strategist says Ben Carroll government at risk of losing more than 30 seats in Saturday’s election, to fall behind Pauline Hanson’s party

blocks.text: The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.
Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.

If replicated across the state, that swing would translate into 67 seats for the Coalition – comfortably above the 45 needed to form a majority government. The Liberals and Nationals currently hold a combined 29 seats.
But the scale of Labor’s defeat remains unclear. Some polls have suggested the party could fall behind One Nation into third place, with its primary vote only marginally ahead of the Greens.

“Right now, definitely, it’s going to be a Coalition government, but how Labor, the Greens and One Nation are going to go – that’s going to be a lot more chaotic,” said Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room.

Raue said One Nation’s prospects will depend heavily on which party it is competing against in each seat. One Nation is targeting 12 lower house seats. It will field candidates in all lower house seats.
In contests with the Liberals or Nationals, One Nation would fare “very badly” because about 80% of preferences from other parties would flow to the Coalition partners, he said.
“The places where they are likely going to be strongest are those outer suburban seats they could take off Labor,” Raue said.
“They probably couldn’t take them if Labor was in a stronger position. Labor is so weak right now that those areas can come into play.”

On Friday, Labor campaign sources said they were bracing for a “wild night”, with three- and four-cornered contests expected across the state. Internal research suggested the party could lose up to 10 seats to One Nation, prompting former premier Steve Bracks to urge voters not to abandon Labor.
One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, tempered expectations, telling reporters on Friday: “We have effectively got one state member, anything more than that is a success. We have already won.”
Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a pollster with Redbridge, said Labor was at risk of losing more than 30 seats – a figure he described as conservative. The party currently holds 54.
“If they come out of this with 20 seats, it’s a really good result,” Samaras said. “Below that, without stating the obvious, it’s a massive problem.”

Samaras said Labor was likely to lose several regional seats, including Ripon, Bendigo East – held by former premier Jacinta Allan – Bendigo West, Eureka and Wendouree. The party could also lose seats across the Geelong region that it has held since 1999, including Bellarine, Geelong, Lara and South Barwon.

In Melbourne’s south-east, Carrum and Frankston were also at risk of switching from Labor to One Nation. Further out, Labor was not in contention in Bass, Hastings and Pakenham, where the contest was shaping as a fight between the Liberals and One Nation, he said.

In the north-west, Melton, Sunbury and Sydenham were also potential One Nation gains. Meanwhile, the Liberals are expected to pick up eastern suburbs seats including Ashwood, Bayswater, Box Hill, Glen Waverley and Ringwood.
The Liberals are even confident in the premier’s own seat of Niddrie and neighbouring Essendon.

Labor’s inner-city seats of Footscray, Northcote and Pascoe Vale were each a “coin toss” between the party and the Greens, Samaras said. But Greens sources are confident about the seats, as well as Prahran, which it lost to the Liberals at a 2025 byelection.
Samaras said the margins in many seats would be fragile.
“The Coalition is going to win 55 to 60 seats but someone only has to breathe in the wrong direction and they lose 20,” he said.
The premier, Ben Carroll, made his final pitch to voters on Friday, saying while Labor had “made some mistakes”, it was the only party on the side of workers in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.

“We won’t fight against you. We won’t make cuts. We certainly won’t say one thing and then, after several million people have voted, then go and do another,” he said, in reference to the Coalition’s pre-budget costings on Thursday, which detailed a plan to privatise the sewage system.
The Coalition leader, Jess Wilson, called the poll a “a referendum on four more years of Labor”.
“Tomorrow Victorians have an opportunity to change the direction of the state we all love and we have the plan to get started,” she said.
If elected on Saturday, she will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

items: Additional reporting by Bertin Huynh and Henry Belot

articles.title: NSW Labor is ‘trampling over party principles’ with preselections by captain’s call, members say
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen was asked by Labor head office not to nominate for Lane Cove in March state election

  • Get our

blocks.text: Labor’s New South Wales leadership has been accused of alienating members and undermining the democratic process, after multiple state election candidates were preselected by “captain’s call” instead of the rank and file.
The premier, Chris Minns, announced on Friday that commercial litigator Jade Tyrrell will be Labor’s candidate for the marginal Liberal-held seat of Lane Cove at March’s state election.
He confirmed the nomination is the latest to be sent to Labor’s national executive, a procedure which bypasses a preselection by branch members.

Guardian Australia understands that Labor’s candidate at the 2023 election, Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen – who reduced the margin of the previously safe Liberal seat by almost two-thirds – was asked not to nominate by Labor head office, in favour of another candidate, Vivienne Moxham-Hall, a former adviser to the health minister, Ryan Park.

After Moxham-Hall – who was subsequently endorsed by local members – withdrew her nomination this month, citing a change in her current workplace policy, Tyrrell has become the second candidate to be chosen for the electorate by party leadership.
A local Labor source said Moxham-Hall and Tyrrell were both highly qualified candidates, but local rank-and-file members had been “strung along” by head office.
“We’ve been trying to win this seat since 2011 and the first time we get close they say all of a sudden, ‘No, we’re imposing a different candidate,’” they said.
In recent weeks, Minns and the party’s organisational wing in Sussex Street have faced accusations of making “captain’s calls” on candidates in multiple winnable or Labor-held seats.

This includes the premier publicly endorsing candidates in seats without rank-and-file preselections, in some cases before the national executive had signed off on them. The candidates in 12 seats for March’s election have been sent to the national executive so far.

Under Labor party rules, the 21-member executive, which includes prime minister Anthony Albanese, can intervene over rank-and-file preselections to choose candidates. While other candidates can still nominate, a recommendation by NSW party leadership in one candidate’s favour is considered a fait accompli.
In the safe Liberal seat of Epping, the premier last week endorsed former Liberal staffer and councillor Tanya Raffoul as Labor’s candidate, a move which has drawn some internal anger.
Although another Labor member Benson Koschinski nominated against Raffoul, the national executive endorsed Raffoul’s candidacy in a unanimous vote.

Guardian Australia understands every member of the executive subbed out to allow proxy voters. NSW minister Rose Jackson subbed in for Albanese, while other proxies included staffers from the premier’s and senior NSW ministers’ offices.

One senior Labor source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said it was not unusual for proxies to be used when ballots were conducted on short notice, but others said it was highly unusual for every single member to nominate one.
Multiple senior branch sources said sending preselections to the national executive had become too regular.
One said it had become “the norm instead of the extraordinary”, while another said it was undermining Labor institutions.
“How does this help the health of the party?” they said.
‘Not running a charity’

In Terrigal, another marginal Liberal seat – and the only one held by the Coalition on the central coast – the deputy premier, Prue Car, on Thursday announced local high school principal Lisa Wicks as Labor’s candidate.
The party’s candidate in 2023, Sam Boughton, had been re-endorsed by members but recently dropped out following a family tragedy and has endorsed Wicks.
Guardian Australia understands that Wicks was first introduced to members at a branch meeting as a new member of the party on Sunday.
after newsletter promotion

In a meeting with members at another local branch on Wednesday – the evening before the announcement – a senior member of Labor’s organisational wing said Wicks would be the party’s candidate after the preselection had been sent to the national executive without any other nominations.

One local member said some at the meeting accepted this, but others supported a preselection “in order for the rank and file to be given their say, after which we would probably have been satisfied with who had been chosen democratically, as is our right”.
A senior Labor party source said the unforeseen circumstances which led to candidates dropping out in Lane Cove and Terrigal had made the use of the national executive necessary.

On Tuesday, Minns said the preselection for Rockdale, a seat held by the sports minister, Steve Kamper, who is a close political ally, would be decided by the executive, following a similar announcement last week about another sitting minister Anoulack Chanthivong.
The intervention in Rockdale has drawn criticism from the former Labor upper house member Shaoquett Moselmane, who said he would have nominated for a rank and file preselection.
“Such action represents yet another example of a party leadership that is increasingly detached from the needs and aspirations of the majority of party members,” he said.
“It’s an act of trampling over party principles of fairness, transparency and honesty in preselection.”

Speaking alongside Tyrrell on Friday, Minns said he understood “concern and consternation about some of those processes”, but cited the threat posed by One Nation which is consistently polling a close second to Labor in NSW.

“I have to put the best team on the path, I have to put outstanding candidates, ones that have got deep connections with the local community, an element of the community that have traditionally voted maybe for a conservative candidate” he said.

Tyrrell, a Labor party member of 15 years, said she had grown up in Hunters Hill, which is in the Lane Cove electorate, and now lived in Waverton, which is in the neighbouring electorate of North Shore.

Guardian Australia understands Pedersen had been involved in monthly street stalls after the 2025 federal election success of local Labor member, Jerome Laxale, but that the party head office had asked for this campaigning to pause earlier this year.

In response to a series of detailed questions sent to NSW Labor head office and the premier, Guardian Australia was referred to comments Minns made at press conferences endorsing the candidates for Winston Hills and Wallsend, both preselections sent to the national executive.
Minns told reporters in Wallsend that Labor was “not running a charity” but a political party.

A Sussex Street source said if the candidates sent to the national executive were elected in March, there would be a “massive injection of talent in Macquarie Street”, including potential future ministers.
Pedersen and Moxham-Hall have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Boatwright debuts strong as Gilas routs Syria in FIBA World Cup qualifiers
articles.summary: New naturalized Filipino Bennie Boatwright and star center Kai Sotto live up to the hype as Gilas Pilipinas pummels Syria to kick off its fifth-window campaign in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Syria had no answer to the towering might and pinpoint shooting of Gilas Pilipinas as the favored Filipino squad rolled to a dominant 97-58 win to begin its campaign in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers fifth window in Seremban, Malaysia on Friday, November 27.

Long-awaited naturalized player Bennie Boatwright made sure to live up to the hype in his national team debut, tallying a big double-double of 16 points and 13 rebounds, while frontcourt partner Kai Sotto led the new twin-tower duo with 18 points and 10 boards in just 17 minutes.

“We only had a few practices with Bennie Boatwright, and yet, he’s fitting into us like a glove,” said Gilas head coach Tim Cone. “He didn’t go out and force anything, and stayed in what we do. From a coaching standpoint, you like it, because it wasn’t guys stepping out of what they do, it was really within what we’ve asked them to do, and that was really nice.”

“I just think that the more Bennie is with us, the more he’ll get comfortable, and know where his teammates are, and know where they like to get the ball. We’ll know more about him as we go along. We just see him elevating his game more and more when he’s with us.”

While Boatwright and Sotto set the tone in the first half on the way to a 43-32 lead, star forward Kevin Quiambao seized the spotlight in the latter two frames, as he led an offensive onslaught from deep to finish with a game-high-tying 18 points, all off a 6-of-8 shooting spree from three.

Thanks to a 29-13 third quarter pullaway that featured a 6-of-7 team clip from downtown, Gilas fully negated its slow start to lead by as many as 40, 95-55, and rise to a 5-4 record in Group E. Syria, meanwhile, stayed at the bottom of the six-nation group with a 2-7 card.
“These games this late in the qualifying, this late window five of six windows, they are so absolutely crucial at this point. We brought by far our best team, I think,” Cone said.

“Our size kind of took over the game at some point. We just controlled the boards. I think we won it like, 60-30, or something like that. When you could do that, you can run up the score, and we were able to run up the score.”After losing to undefeated Australia (9-0), earlier in the day, 84-67, Iran fell to a 5-4 slate ahead of its crucial clash on Sunday, November 29, against Gilas, which now enjoys a three-game winning streak after losing four straight.

A sweep of the Malaysia leg can put the Philippines on top of its Iranian rivals to boost its chances of World Cup qualification after a stretch of heartbreaking windows. Gilas ends its qualifying run at home in Cebu City in late February 2027.
Gilas Pilipinas 97 – Sotto 18, Quiambao 18, Boatwright 16, Gomez de Liaño 11, Perez 10, Phillips 10, Ramos 5, Edu 4, Millora-Brown 4, Newsome 1, Thompson 0, Rosario 0.

articles.title: German lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
articles.summary: German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has…

image.caption: German lawmakers are set to vote on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spendingImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 27, 2026
German parliament passes 2027 budget

Germany's ‌lower ⁠house ⁠of parliament, the Bundestag, ​voted in favor ​a €556 ​billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost ​defense ​and infrastructure spending.
Total new borrowing will reach €210 ​billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in ​2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild ​its military after decades of underinvestment.
"It is right that we invest in the railways and ​in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday. "It is right... that we invest in our security."

German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.
"We are putting up the ⁠money for ​defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil said. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again."

articles.title: Thanksgiving meal in Florida leads to ‘mass casualty’ food poisoning incident
articles.summary:
Local media reported that 18 people fell ill after attending a Thanksgiving lunch at a medical center headquarters

A Thanksgiving meal in Florida triggered a bout of food poisoning so bad…

blocks.text: A Thanksgiving meal in Florida triggered a bout of food poisoning so bad that local emergency officials said it was a “mass casualty” event as numerous stricken diners were sent to hospital.
Local media reported that 18 people at the Leon Medical Center headquarters in Doral fell ill due to possible food poisoning after attending the center’s annual Thanksgiving lunch on Wednesday.

Miami-Dade fire rescue crews who received reports of the possible food poisoning said the call was upgraded to a “mass casualty incident” after 15 of those who fell ill required hospitalization, the Miami Herald reported.
In a statement to NBC Miami Leon Medical Center said: “Some of the staff began to experience gastrointestinal symptoms shortly after the luncheon and required treatment.”
“We continue to work with the caterers to determine, if possible, the cause and continue to provide support to our staff and their families.”
No patients at the center were affected. Investigations are continuing as to the exact cause and nature of the food poisoning.

articles.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.summary: The endangered reptiles were bound with duct tape to prevent them moving, officials say.

blocks.text: Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles, external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases, external. Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

articles.title: Cow’s milk sales at record low in Britain as people opt for plant-based options
articles.summary:
Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives

Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with…

blocks.text: Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began.

Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974.

So why are people buying less? One reason, say experts, is that the growing accessibility of plant-based milks has created a mindset shift when it comes to dairy – with even meat-eaters changing their habits.

“You can get plant-based milk in a lot of different places now and the taste isn’t that different,” says Rosie Green, a professor of environment, food and health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. “People might be worried about animal welfare as well – and then the environmental problems are the icing on the cake.”

Mass produced dairy has a huge impact on the climate. From their digestion and manure, cows emit methane, a gas the government has called a “super pollutant” because it is more potent than carbon dioxide and plays a big role in global heating. The agriculture sector represents 48% of the UK’s methane emissions, with 78% of those produced by cattle.

“But the thing people pay less attention to is [dairy’s] land use footprint, because dairy cows require a lot of land for grazing,” says Ruth Westcott, the director of campaigns at Foodrise. They also require feed, some of which is grown on UK cropland and some imported. Westcott says the shift towards larger, more intensive dairy farms has increased reliance on imported feed.

Experts say animal welfare is another reason why people are turning off cow’s milk as consumers learn more about standard practices in the dairy industry, such as the early removal of calves from their mothers. “People are becoming more aware of what happens on dairy farming,” Sean Barrs, a senior campaigner at Animal Justice Project, says. “They’re seeing more images on the internet of what it looks like and they’re becoming more educated.”

As tastes for cow’s milk have declined, purchases of plant-based alternatives have grown, from an average 37ml to 94ml a week since 2014. The food trends expert Morgaine Gaye says plant milks are no long seen as a “vegan choice” but “an everybody choice”.

“There’s lots of people who eat meat, are not even vegetarian, but have a non-dairy milk in their coffee, have an oat milk on their cereal, just for the taste, because they’ve been exposed to it so much,” she says.

High street shops have played their part in that exposure. The Canteen on Stokes Croft in Bristol stopped selling meat dishes in 2020. This year, they began offering oat to customers before cow’s when serving hot drinks. “We word it like: ‘Do you want oat milk or dairy?’ That really changed habits,” says Liam Stocks, the general manager. “A lot of customers will go: ‘Oh, I will have oats.’ You’re making them feel like it’s the default.”

Stocks says the decline in purchases of cow’s milk speaks to a broader attitude change. “It’s an easy win, right? If you are wanting to be more environmentally friendly, it’s very hard to stop eating meat. I always see [cutting dairy] as a first thing people might do to try and change their behaviour.”

With searing temperatures and collapsing climate talks at the forefront of the discussion, it can be easy to forget how transforming food systems is also imperative to tackling the climate crisis. “Changing your diet is the one thing that most people can do that will have the biggest impact on the environment,” says Westcott. “The climate impacts of our diets have stayed stubbornly high and barely reduced at all since 1990. We’re just not seeing anywhere near the changes that we need.”

The decline in liquid-milk purchases has not meant less milk is being produced. UK production reached a record in 2025, with more milk going into cheese, yoghurt, butter and powders as demand for some of those products grew, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB).
In its latest carbon budget, the government for the first time targeted a reduction in dairy consumption, aiming for a 20% cut by 2035.

Producing less dairy would be a huge step towards sustaining our food systems. Westcott says: “Reducing dairy consumption would free up land in the UK for nature recovery or for growing more food directly for human consumption, like more lentils, peas, beans – more high-protein foods that would allow us to be more food resilient and have a higher domestic food production and need to import less.”

For Green, swapping milk is an easy way to make that difference. “We can’t reach our environmental targets no matter how much we do in transport or energy generation – we have to change the food system as well,” she says. “We need to still eat less meat as well – but switching the milk is a good start.”

Dairy UK, the industry body, says its Dairy Roadmap, run with AHDB and the NFU, has cut the greenhouse gas emissions associated with milk production by 24% since 2008. “The dairy sector plays a significant role in the UK,” according to their website. “Our processing members play a vital role inemploying 22,500 people at processing sites around the country. On top of that, dairy farms employ 50,000 more people, both directly and in supporting industries.
“British consumers show their love for dairy every day. If any evidence were needed to prove that, the fact that 96% of adults buy milk should be proof enough.”

articles.title: As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
articles.summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.

image.caption: Barrow came ‌to power in 2017 after defeating longtime ruler Yahya JammehImage: ZOHRA BENSEMRA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.
President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and four other candidates.
The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.
What matters to voters
Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.
A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.

"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."

blocks.caption: Many Gambians have voiced concerns about a lack of economic opportunitiesImage: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

blocks.text: Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.
Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.
"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.
Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.
"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.

"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.
Jobs, cost of living top of mind
Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.
What happens when you speak up?
The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.
The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.
The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.
Alhagie Sama, a voter in Banjul, said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.

"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.
Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.
"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.
"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."
Election under observation
The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.

The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.
International observers are also monitoring the process.
Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.
Gambia Election 2026: Can the opposition win?
The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.
"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.

Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."
The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

articles.title: On the arrest of Informer TV owner and editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
articles.summary: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable or whether this is another political power…

image.caption: Dragan J. Vucicevic, owner and editor-in-chief of Informer TV, was arrested on November 25 and remanded in custody for 30 days. He is pictured here earlier this monthImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June last year.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by the police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching" and he labelled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures" and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted political opponents of the previous government, activists and independent journalists.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

blocks.caption: Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC…

blocks.text: "This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

blocks.caption: Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting licenseImage: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

blocks.caption: On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of InformerImage: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

blocks.text: Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.
A reckoning or an internal power struggle?
Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.
The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

articles.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful…

image.caption: Duterte was elected president in 2016 following a populist campaign in which he promised to kill criminals and drug dealersImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.
It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.
Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.
Why is Duterte on trial?
Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.
During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.
Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte
However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.
A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.
"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.
Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.
His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.
"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.
Why was Duterte arrested?
Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.
The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.
For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.
What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.
Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.
Philippine cafe keeps alive memory of 'drug war' victims

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.
Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.
In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.
What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.
Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.
DW speaks with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.
Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.
For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.
"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

articles.title: With World Cup and Olympic berths at stake, revamped Canadian women's team could begin new chapter
articles.summary: With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships this Saturday, the Canadian women’s national team can clinch a berth to the 2027 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

image.caption: Canada's Kaylee Hunter, left, shown in action during a match against Denmark on Oct. 9, is part of the Canadian women's national team that will be looking for a crucial win over Panama this weekend at the CONCACAF W Championship. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Soccer·Preview
With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships this Saturday, the Canadian women’s national team can clinch a berth to the 2027 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Canadians face Panama at the CONCACAF W championships on Saturday in Houston
The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup proved to the world that Canada is a soccer nation.
This Saturday, at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium, the Canadian women’s national team can amplify that reputation.
With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships, the women’s side has a chance to clinch a berth to the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

That entails decisively conquering an opponent they beat 1-0 in 2022 — which came with an allegation of “spying” levied against them. The complaint never reached the disciplinary committee because there was no evidence.

Canada has won the continental tournament twice before but is looking to secure qualification to next year's World Cup hosted by Brazil. The Canadians are placed ninth by FIFA rankings, and Panama is 54th.

While there is always a pause to think about the worst-case scenario, the Canadian women's team goes into this tournament very well prepared. Their recent series against Denmark left with one win (in penalty shots) and one loss but a lot of lessons learned. After a loss 4-3 against Denmark on Thanksgiving Monday at BMO Field in Toronto, head coach Casey Stoney told the media that it was necessary to “keep context and not panic.”

items: Canada's women's soccer team can kill two birds with one stone

blocks.text: Context is essential for this tournament and Stoney understands what is at stake.

It is not impossible for Canada to qualify for the World Cup nor the Olympics if they don’t win against Panama, but the path is far more difficult. A journey that Stoney and the team would likely want to avoid.

Stoney, a legend on England’s national women’s team with 130 caps, learned some hard lessons, on losing in transition and the need to kill the game quickly. Something they will need to do with Panama.
Canada’s storied backline will not have Vanessa Gilles, one of its strongest players, who is unavailable due to injury.

But this team will boast a fresh and clinical group of attackers — something missing from previous iterations of this team after the retirement of the world's top international goal scorer and Canada’s skipper, Christine Sinclair, in 2023.
Kaylee Hunter, the 18-year old phenom from Calgary, will be back with a team of seasoned players including Jessie Fleming, 2026 NWSL Defender of the Year Janine Sonis, and Kadeisha Buchanan.

items: Meet budding Canadian soccer star Olivia Smith: ‘The potential to be one of the best in the world’

blocks.text: Hunter just renewed her contract with AFC Toronto in the Northern Super League (NSL). She made a name for herself on the international stage when she scored a hat trick against France at the U20 Women’s World Cup in Poland during the September window.

Hunter is the top youth player in the country and has chosen to stay in Canada and compete at the highest level. This is a particularly poignant move after Hunter was part of the AFC Toronto club that won the Diana B. Matheson Cup after beating the Montreal Roses in the NSL Final.

The Canadian women's national side features five players from Canada’s domestic league, including fellow attacker Delaney Baie Pridham — who scored her first international goal in the Toronto match against Denmark.

The attacking line is punctuated by Olivia Smith of Arsenal FC, and also midfielder Simi Awujo of Manchester United FC, both of whom are enjoying success in goal scoring and in wins in the Women’s Super League (WSL).
Marie-Yasmine (Mimi) Alidou plays midfield for the Montreal Roses and will support attackers as club rivalries are put aside for the country. All need to be finding the back of the net.

items: Buchanan, Smith highlight Canadian women's roster for World Cup, Olympic qualifier

blocks.text: Instead of turning a new leaf of attacking prowess, Canada should be thinking about planting deep roots, says Amy Walsh, soccer commentator and former captain of the national team.
Walsh, a Canada Soccer Hall of Fame inductee, says that a new approach doesn't have to be drastic, but this team has to find its form.

“It has to reaffirm its identity as one of the toughest teams to play against, that lock down defensively,” Walsh said. “So you put [clinical finishers and defensive strength] together, and I think it allows this foundational style of play, this philosophy, to take shape and put down roots.”
The women's national team has not beaten a top 15-ranked team in Stoney’s tenure that began in January 2025.
A shift away from former mainstays

With a change in roster announcements and the exclusion of players who were once considered mainstays, the shift is important considering what is at stake. Nichelle Prince (119 caps with the senior team) was named as a practice player.
“Those conversations are not easy to have,” Stoney admitted on a media call following the squad announcement. Stoney said that when she spoke with Prince, she said it was Prince’s choice.
Another player to not make the roster was Adriana Leon (132 caps).

Stoney said it was simply because Leon had not featured regularly at her club San Diego FC. She says that getting “consistent minutes” is a priority in selection. Game experience offers an opportunity to stay sharp for an intense campaign with the national team, preparedness in fitness, and practiced in game IQ.
Is Canada ready? CANWNT roster revealed & CANMNT 2026 report card
This is the first match with consequences that the Canadian women's national program has played since 2024. They have had international friendlies but nothing this consequential.

Stoney says that they have spent a lot of time preparing and want to qualify for both Brazil and Los Angeles, but also challenge the United States for the CONCACAF title. A win against the reigning CONCACAF W champions would boost their confidence moving towards a World Cup year.
Walsh agreed that the team is up for the challenge.

“I think they come into this understanding what's on the line, and I think they're very well prepared, and they understand the task in front of them, but they also understand how to get success playing ‘Stoney Ball.’”
Stoney Ball considers that structural pieces can be tweaked but also how a “team-first mentality” is essential.
The team has faced ups and downs but its culture and identity are one that has always carried a firm belief in the collective.
With this next chapter for Canada, the game plan must be to demonstrate how lethal, decisive and unflappable it can be.
Stoney leads the charge with seasoned vets and young blood to write a new chapter for Canada women’s soccer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Shireen Ahmed is a multi-platform sports journalist, a TEDx speaker, mentor, and an award-winning sports activist who focuses on the intersections of racism and misogyny in sports. She is an industry expert on Muslim women in sports, and her academic research and contributions have been widely published. She is co-creator and co-host of the “Burn It All Down” feminist sports podcast team. In addition to being a seasoned investigative reporter, her commentary is featured by media outlets in Canada, the USA, Europe and Australia. She holds an MA in Media Production from Toronto Metropolitan University where she now teaches Sports Journalism and Sports Media. You can find Shireen tweeting or drinking coffee, or tweeting about drinking coffee. She lives with her four children and her cat.

articles.title: DOH eyes faster upgrades for LGU-run hospitals in 2027
articles.summary: The Senate finance committee recommends an additional P5.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, pushing its proposed 2027 allocation to P15.58 billion

blocks.text: DOH. The Department of Health facade.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
The Senate finance committee recommends an additional P5.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, pushing its proposed 2027 allocation to P15.58 billion

items: The Department of Health plans to decentralize funding for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program by 2027.
The Senate finance committee recommended increasing the proposed 2027 budget for HFEP to P15.58 billion.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Health plans to bring funds for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) down to the provincial level in 2027, to speed up infrastructure projects and the decongestion of DOH-run hospitals.

The Senate finance committee recommended an additional P5.4 billion for HFEP, pushing the proposed allocation to P15.58 billion, Senator JV Ejercito said during plenary deliberations on the DOH’s proposed 2027 budget on Friday, November 27.

This comes after the House of Representatives approved only P10.09 billion for HFEP in its version of the general appropriations bill (HGAB), lower than the P14.54 billion allocated in the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“Admittedly, ‘yong pagiging centralized ay talaga naging problema…for the whole fund to be utilized. Kaya nga po siguro one reason ‘yan [na] P4 billion natanggal sa HGAB,” said Ejercito, the Senate finance committee chairman and the DOH’s budget sponsor.

“But dito sa ating committee, binalik natin dahil may bagong programa ang DOH under Secretary [Edwin] Mercado, that is to download ito sa provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will [be improved, capacitated], para po ma-decongest ‘yong DOH-run hospitals,” he added.

(Admittedly, HFEP being centralized became a problem for the whole fund to be utilized. Maybe that’s one reason why P4 billion was cut from the HGAB. But the Senate finance committee restored it because the DOH, under Secretary Edwin Mercado, has a new program, that is to download the funding to provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will be improved, capacitated, and to decongest the DOH-run hospitals).
With the limited funding, the DOH will also be prioritizing the completion of ongoing HFEP projects, particularly critical health facilities in remote and disadvantaged areas.

Ejercito said DOH-run hospitals, which are end-referral centers providing advanced or specialty care, currently have an average bed occupancy rate of 150%, especially with the implementation of zero balance billing (ZBB).

Since the ZBB rollout in July 2025, 4.2 million patients have benefited from the program in DOH-run hospitals, according to Ejercito. Recently, it was piloted in some hospitals run by local government units (LGUs).

In its version, the Senate realigned P19.8 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations or AICS, to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.

Ejercito previously said the funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the ZBB program. This includes P7.6 billion for DOH hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for LGU hospitals.

Aside from boosting the HFEP budget, the Senate also provided an additional P1.099 billion for health promotion, P1.599 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu Transition Program.
But if Senator Panfilo Lacson had his way, essential health programs would get even more funds while MAP would become a thing of the past.
MAP, previously called Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients or MAIFIP, has been tagged by watchdogs as “soft pork” and called a “politicized discretionary program.”

Acknowledging that the Senate might have to wrestle with the House regarding unfunding MAP, Lacson suggested introducing a special provision that would allow the remaining P16.2 billion for MAP in the proposed 2027 budget to be allocated to the chambers’ public assistance centers instead. He proposed having DOH personnel oversee the vetting process for claiming the medical aid.
Lacson said this was in a bid to eventually phase out the aid program.

“For next year, the DOH is planning to have a rules-based approach in granting medical assistance to qualified patients. They will, of course, study ‘yong inyong (your) proposal,” Ejercito replied. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
articles.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

image.caption: Early marriage often disrupts girls' education and opportunities Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.
The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.
"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.
What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.
The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.
Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.
But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.
When marriage becomes an economic calculation
The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.
In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.
Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women
Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.
War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.
Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.
Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.
"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.
Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.
What can be done to protect girls?
Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.
"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.
According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.
