articles.title: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline
articles.summary: Department for Work and Pensions officials say welfare payments will continue to be made despite huge outage

blocks.text: Almost all pensions and benefits systems in the UK are unavailable following a “cyber incident”.

Anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit was not able to do so on Friday morning. Department for Work and Pensions officials say payments will continue to be made as normal.
The cause of the incident, and whether it is the result of a cyber-attack, is not publicly known but the department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre.
It comes days after the government issued an alert warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.

The department said in a statement: “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.”
The DWP’s most senior official told a committee of MPs this month that cybersecurity and resilience was one of the issues “that keeps a new permanent secretary awake”.

Sarah Healey, the DWP permanent secretary, was appearing before the work and pensions select committee, where she was asked who would ensure that DWP systems would “not be the frontline in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin”.

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this month, with their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F), in what was blamed on a cyber-attack. The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The Labour MP Liam Byrne, the chair of the Commons business, innovation, science and trade committee, said it was too early to comment on the cause, but told Sky News: “In this new world that we are in cyber-attacks are going to be more prevalent.

“So we are going to have to upgrade our cybersecurity. if you are running particularly a small business you need to be more cyber aware these days. Let’s hope they get the DWP systems back up online.”

articles.title: AI can combine mathematical ideas on a scale beyond individual human minds. But could it produce ideas likes Einstein?
articles.summary: It once struggled to get simple sums right. But AI is now tackling tough mathematical problems like the Riemann hypothesis. How AI made this extraordinary leap. And why mathematicians should be…

image.caption: The rise of AI is raising questions about which mathematical skills humans will need to develop in the futureImage: picture alliance / ZUMAPRESS.com

blocks.text: Last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.
A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he told me, often get simple calculations wrong.

Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.
That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.
How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?
Why was AI so bad at math?
The answer lies in how AI processes information, said Andrea Asperti, a computer scientist at Italy's University of Bologna.
Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.
Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.

"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.
Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.
"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.
How AI got so much better at math
Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.
AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.

blocks.caption: Claude can work with specialized mathematical software to generate and verify formal proofs, rather than relying solely on its language capabilitiesImage: Thomas Trutschel/IMAGO

blocks.text: "What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti said.
Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.
"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti said.
Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.
"I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were; AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.
What makes AI so good at math
Ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.

"When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono said.
Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.
"Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono said.
The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.
And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.
How AI is changing the working world

Ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii."
He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.
"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono said.
A 'superhuman' achievement
Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.
"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he said.
Ono called the achievement "superhuman."
Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.
Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.
AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti said.
'Deep worry' for mathematicians' future
Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.
Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.
"But now we live at a time where — shoot for the moon. The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time."
"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that."
Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.
"Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he said.
Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra."

blocks.caption: Einstein transformed our understanding of space and time. Could AI independently make a comparable scientific breakthrough?Image: United Archives/kpa Keystone/IMAGO

blocks.text: How mathematicians can rethink their role
In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.
"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," said Buzzard, "so we need new methods."
Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.
"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he said.
But, he said, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button."
So, that is the issue of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?

Ono said: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet."

articles.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps, but face hurdles and risks
articles.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them…

image.caption: Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, is seeking skilled professionals in a number of sectors Image: Gunter Hübner/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.
He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.
Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.
India meets German engineering
Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

But Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly the renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), remain hesitant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.
The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.
This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.
Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage
Language a key hurdle
Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency, but soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.
David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.
Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.
Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."
Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.
Delivered! — The courier driver business
Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?
German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.
But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.
The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the EU for workers.

These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.
The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.
"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.
While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.
"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."
Cost of a dream: Indian students in Germany
Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."
What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?
Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.
In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.
"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

articles.title: Robin Padilla faces DOJ investigation for obstruction of justice complaint
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla on Friday went to the Department of Justice to attend the preliminary investigation on the obstruction of justice complaint filed against him in connection with the alleged…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 6:50pm

Senator Robin Padilla on Friday went to the Department of Justice to attend the preliminary investigation on the obstruction of justice complaint filed against him in connection with the alleged escape of Senator Bato dela Rosa from the Senate building.
In a video by Sandra Aguinaldo of GMA News, Julius Henry Balteza, Padilla’s legal counsel, said they are filing a rejoinder in response to the complainant’s reply to their counter-affidavit.
Balteza maintained that Padilla was innocent of the allegations against him.
“For our defense, we maintain na lang ‘yung earlier answers namin na we will not be divulging our answers. Pero to answer that, yes, we maintain po ‘yung innocence ni Senator Padilla,” he said.
(For our defense, we will maintain our previous answer that we will not divulge our answers. But to answer that, yes, we maintain Senator Padilla's innocence.)

On May 28, the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP-CIDG) filed a complaint for obstruction of justice against Padilla and others with the DOJ over the escape of Senator Ronald "Bato" Dela Rosa from the Senate building.

Dela Rosa is the subject of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for “alleged criminal responsibility as an indirect co-perpetrator” in the crimes against humanity of murder during the Duterte administration's war on drugs. He was then chief of the Philippine National Police.
He sought refuge at the Senate on May 11 after authorities attempted to serve the said arrest warrant. However, he slipped out of the Senate building on May 14.
Padilla previously maintained that he did not help Dela Rosa “escape,” as the former police chief only asked to hitch a ride with him out of the Senate building on May 14. —Jamil Santos/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: King tides batter US coasts as storms threaten Thanksgiving celebrations
articles.summary:
Heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding creating hazardous conditions for millions travelling for holiday

King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a…

blocks.text: King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a turbulent Thanksgiving period, with severe weather threatening millions across the country. Along the California coast, king tides caused considerable damage. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, large waves battered the coastline on Wednesday, destroying part of a pier and sending debris into the ocean.

The National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings covering parts of the Pacific coastline and shorelines around San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay. Several beachfront properties in Pacifica have already experienced flooding, while authorities in Marin County temporarily issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront homes at Stinson Beach.

The high tides also affected southern California. San Diego recorded a tide of 8ft 11in (2.7 metres) on Wednesday morning, while Los Angeles experienced tides reaching approximately 8.19ft, potentially surpassing a record set at the end of October.

blocks.caption: A flooded street in Sea Isle City, New Jersey. Photograph: Seetheview.com/Reuters

blocks.text: King tides are unusually high natural tides that occur when the gravitational forces of the sun and moon combine around their alignment with Earth. Their impact is being heightened by unusually warm Pacific waters associated with the 2026 super El Niño.

A Nor’easter has also been bringing severe weather across the eastern US. The system produced heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding, creating hazardous conditions for millions of Americans travelling to celebrate the holiday.

The severity of the forecast forced an unprecedented decision in New York: Macy’s postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, until Saturday. It was the first time in the event’s history that the parade had been postponed because of weather. The decision was taken to safeguard performers and spectators, particularly given the dangers that powerful gusts pose to the parade’s enormous character balloons.

Meanwhile, significant fresh snowfall during the past week has transformed conditions across several major ski regions in the Alps, providing an excellent early season foundation for the new season. French resorts have been among the biggest beneficiaries. Reported accumulated snow depths on Thursday included approximately 120cm in the Tignes-Val d’Isère area, while substantial snowfall was recorded around Les Deux Alpes, Alpe d’Huez and the Les Trois Vallées. Further snowfall is forecast across parts of France, Switzerland, Italy and Austria, with several resorts expecting additional accumulations over the coming days.

articles.title: Momentous decision awaits after judges’ call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
articles.summary:
Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called…

blocks.text: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

articles.title: Supreme Court set to deliver ruling on Quebec's secularism law

image.caption: People watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: What’s at stake as the Supreme Court rules on Quebec’s secularism law

The Supreme Court of Canada will make its decision on Quebec’s Bill 21 and could rule on the government’s pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clause. The bill, enacted in 2019, bars some public workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols on the job. Friday’s ruling could also set new rules for how provinces across Canada can use the notwithstanding clause.

items: November 27Arguments for and against the bill — and what's at stake todayWhy all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21Quebec’s Bill 21 bans religious symbols for some civil servants. Now, the legal battle has shifted from the ban itself to whether the province overstepped by invoking the notwithstanding clause in the text of the law, to bypass Charter rights.I covered the Supreme Court hearings of the Bill 21 case last spring for CBC Montreal, and I'll be covering the decision today. Let's talk a bit about what's at stake.First, there's the simple question of whether the ban on wearing religious symbols at work for some Quebec civil servants will be maintained or struck down. The overwhelming majority of people affected by Bill 21 and subsequent secularism laws are Muslim women who wear hijabs. Some teachers in Quebec have lost their jobs because of the ban, others have seen their careers stalled, and people studying to be teachers have abandoned that career path.But this case goes beyond the religious symbols ban. It's become much more about how the Quebec government used the constitutional notwithstanding clause to shield the ban from legal challenges.

How Bill 21 reached the Supreme CourtHolly CabreraPeople watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)Today's ruling marks the latest chapter of a seven-year legal battle. In June 2019, the province's majority Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government passed Bill 21, An Act Respecting the Laicity of the State, and pre-emptively invoked the notwithstanding clause — which is contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms — to shield it from court challenges. The English Montreal School Board contested the law in Quebec Superior Court that October.In April 2021, Justice Marc-André Blanchard largely upheld the legislation, save for two exceptions: one for English-language school boards and another allowing National Assembly members to wear face coverings while sitting. The Quebec Court of Appeal overturned the exemption for English-language school boards in 2024, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed to hear appeals in January 2025, setting the stage for today's decision.

Supreme Court to rule on Quebec's secularism lawHolly CabreraThe Supreme Court of Canada as seen from Parliament Hill in Ottawa. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)Canada's top court is getting ready to rule on Quebec's Bill 21, after spending months deliberating the province's secularism law.The case was heard over four days in March, making it one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court of Canada. A record 51 interveners took part in the proceedings, including six attorneys general. Bill 21 prevents employees in positions of authority in Quebec, such as teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols while on the job, and also requires civil servants to keep their faces uncovered when providing services. We'll bring you the decision as soon as the embargo lifts at 9:45 a.m. ET, along with the ensuing reaction and analysis.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
articles.summary: The Ugandan army is helping the Congolese military fight an Islamist militant group in the east of the country.

blocks.text: The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero town.

Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".

Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.

Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

articles.title: Sara Duterte decries dad Rodrigo's required attendance in ICC trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday said it was "unfair" that her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, is being required to attend trial proceedings for his crimes against humanity case before…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 6:36pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday said it was "unfair" that her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, is being required to attend trial proceedings for his crimes against humanity case before the International Criminal Court (ICC) on a daily basis.
Speaking before the media, the vice president stressed that her father is already 81 years old and is unlikely to focus throughout an eight-hour trial.
"I think it's unfair that they are demanding that he attends the trial every day as long as there is a trial, because of his age. Clearly, he cannot sit eight hours a day on a chair," she said.
"And I don't think he can focus and give his time and attention, particularly his attention, to something for eight hours. So I think it's unfair to demand that of an 81-year-old man," she added.
The vice president expressed hope that the court would allow her father to attend the trial virtually.
"Unfortunately, that was not given him, so I hope that his defense team will ask for that in the coming days," she said.
The ICC Chamber III earlier found the elder Duterte fit to stand trial, stating that he "is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings."
The court chamber also ordered measures to facilitate Duterte's participation in the proceedings.
The trial is scheduled to open on November 30, 2026.
However, Sara Duterte stood firm that she is not expecting a fair trial from the ICC.

"Particularly because this is the only remaining case in the ICC already. And I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, they would want to make a statement that they are in the right," she said.
"So there is no one else there that they would like to make a statement to, and that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," she added.
Trial aside, the vice president said she and her family have no complaints as to how the ICC is treating Rodrigo in the detention unit.
She said the Scheveningen Prison in The Hague, Netherlands has been "taking good care" of the former president. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ex media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
articles.summary: The former Murdoch media executive was overheard at an event referring to the way Grace Tame was dressed.

blocks.text: An Australian media mogul has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

articles.title: Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
articles.summary: Violent clashes mar a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.

blocks.text: Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.

In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."

Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."

Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
Besiktas won the match 2-1.

"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.

The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.

At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.

"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."

articles.title: DBM releases P336M for hog raisers affected by ASF
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has released P336 million to fund the compensation of hog raisers affected by African swine fever (ASF).

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 6:13pm
The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has released P336 million to fund the compensation of hog raisers affected by African swine fever (ASF).

During the interpellation of the Department of Agriculture's (DA) budget at the Senate plenary, Senator Risa Hontiveros raised that more than 8,400 hog raisers and traders affected by ASF from 2023 to 2026 have yet to be paid by the government for their losses. They are owed a total of P434 million.

Senator Francis Pangilinan, the DA's budget sponsor in the Senate, said the DBM had not released the contingency fund. However, Pangilinan was informed on the spot that DBM released the fund on Thursday night. He quipped that perhaps the agency knew that Hontiveros was about to ask that question.
"So P336 million has been released, unpaid is P229 million as of 2024, and December, the payout will start," Pangilinan said.
The remaining balance will be sourced from quick response funds, Pangilinan said. The balance will be fully paid by the end of the first quarter of 2027.
"Just for the record, your Committee on Agriculture has been following this up since July. And after five months, it has been released," said Pangilinan in a mix of English and Filipino.
ASF first hit the Philippines in 2019, severely affecting the country's hog industry and reducing its swine population from around 13 million heads to about 8 million.
The Bureau of Animal Industry has reported ASF outbreaks in 76 of the country's 82 provinces. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Bong Revilla's bail affirmed by Sandiganbayan
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan on Friday denied the Ombudsman"s appeal to reverse the court"s July 31 decision granting the bail petition filed by former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, Jr., saying that the…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 6:08pm

The Sandiganbayan on Friday denied the Ombudsman’s appeal to reverse the court’s July 31 decision granting the bail petition filed by former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, Jr., saying that the prosecution’s evidence linking him to flood control kickback was not strong.
This stemmed from the P92.8-million malversation case filed against Revilla over a flood control project that was found to have no actual physical structure.

The Sandiganbayan said that Revilla’s role in supposedly ensuring that the said project would be funded under the General Appropriations Act is not the job of one person, given that the said proposed national budget is collectively approved by the House, the Senate, and the bicameral conference committee.

“The court maintained that the evidence adduced by the prosecution to prove overt acts of conspiracy on the part of accused Revilla was not strong. His (Revilla) participation in the legislative process was diluted and attenuated by the composition and structure of the Philippine Congress, as well as several institutional stages (or veto points) which a policy proposal must go through before its enactment as a law,” the Sandiganbayan said.

“Thus, it could not infer the overt act of facilitation from accused Revilla's Senate membership and Public Works Committee chairpersonship. Consequently, the chain of inference leading to the existence of conspiracy on the part of accused Revilla was broken,” it added.
Likewise, the anti-graft court cited that the case filed against Revilla would require malversation of public funds for a conviction, which the prosecution failed to prove during the bail hearings.

“The boxes of cash allegedly received by accused Revilla came from a pool of funds coming from private contractors. Even with testimonies narrating the general scheme within the Department of Public Works and Highways, the fundamental principle of in dubio pro reo (in applying and interpreting penal laws, to resolve all doubts in favor of the accused) would foreclose the characterization of these advance kickbacks as "public funds or property" in the context of malversation,” the Sandiganbayan said.

“Even if it were to be assumed that the prosecution had managed to adduce strong evidence of guilt that accused Revilla may have received cash from the private contractors, the same would only tend to prove the existence of bribery-an offense that is bailable as a matter of right regardless of whether the same is direct or indirect,” it added.
Further, the Sandiganbayan Third Division also denied the appeals for bail of Revilla’s co-accused.
These include former DPWH officials, namely: Brice Ericson Hernandez, Arjay Domasig, Jaypee Mendoza, Juanito Mendoza, Emelita Juat and Christina Pineda.
The anti-graft court said Revilla's co-accused did not dispute the prosecution’s allegations that the P92.8 million flood control project in Pandi, Bulacan was never built.

“As to accused Hernandez, Domasig, Jaypee and Juanito Mendoza, Juat, and Pineda, the Court ruled on the basis of the evidence of the prosecution considering that they had chosen to forgo their right to present rebuttal evidence. The discrepancy between the physical state of the subject project and the public records pertaining thereto, which the accused had signed in their official capacities as accountable officers, was strong evidence of their guilt of the crime of malversation,” the Sandiganbayan said.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: German Catholic Church: Abuse victims may receive higher compensation
articles.summary: In a landmark ruling, judges in Cologne found the Catholic Church responsible for abuse committed by clergy members. Victims could now be entitled to more compensation.

image.caption: In the Archdiocese of Cologne, there have been numerous instances of sexualized violence committed by priestsImage: Christoph Hardt/Panama Pictures/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.

The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priest for several years.
Melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.

blocks.caption: Melanie F. was subjected to serious sexual abuse in the late 1970s and early 1980sImage: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Abortion carried out without consent

In determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges said that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.

Born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.

Beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.

In its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.

The Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.

The 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.
Catholic Church faces flurry of US abuse cases
The Church's position served as a 'cover'
But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed.
In their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection.

His role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.

After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it."
The Archdiocese of Cologne said it "respectfully" took note of the decision.

The perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.

"The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.

From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.
As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing
'A day of hope for survivors of sexual abuse'

Schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards.
However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he said, describing the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches."
Matthias Katsch, spokesperson for the survivor advocacy group Eckiger Tisch, also called the ruling "good news."

"Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he said. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences.

"The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he said, allowing the crimes to happen. Melanie F. had sought compensation of between €800,000 and €900,000.

In March 2026, the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments (UKA), which was established by the German Bishops' Conference in 2021, announced that it had approved payments totaling approximately €93 million for survivors in all dioceses. Since then, several dioceses have published additional studies containing new reports of abuse cases.

Sixteen years after survivors and Jesuit priest Klaus Mertes helped bring the abuse scandal to light, the German Bishops' Conference will now have to prepare for significantly higher compensation payments.
Churches should reach out to survivors

In the United States, where civil lawsuits seeking compensation often involve far higher sums than in Germany, a number of Catholic dioceses have filed for bankruptcy. But that is unlikely to happen in Germany. The Bonn-based law firm of Eberhard Luetjohann, Melanie F.'s attorney, has reported receiving inquiries from hundreds of abuse survivors seeking higher compensation.

Spokesperson for Eckiger Tisch, Matthias Katsch, called on church leaders to engage in dialogue with survivors and their advocacy groups. Katsch said the question of the Church's liability for crimes committed by priests lies at the heart of most cases in which survivors are dissatisfied with the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments' decisions and believe they are entitled to higher compensation.
It is unacceptable, he said, that these survivors must go to court to obtain the compensation they deserve.
This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

articles.title: Thanksgiving storm on U.S. East Coast knocks out power, disrupts flights
articles.summary: A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the U.S. East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power to nearly 1 million customers at one point as wind gusts of up to 112 km/h…

image.caption: New York postponed the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday over fears of extreme weather, a first in the event's 100-year history, as a major storm gathered steam on the U.S. East Coast. (Kena Betancur AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the U.S. East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power to nearly 1 million customers at one point as wind gusts of up to 112 km/h toppled trees and power lines.
More than 900,000 U.S. utility customers had no power Thursday evening

The storm contributed to flight delays, with FlightAware reporting a total of 454 U.S.-related cancellations on Thursday and 2,411 delays. Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit.
Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned of an increased risk of falling trees and power outages.
More than 908,000 U.S. utility customers had no power as of 9:56 p.m. ET, according to PowerOutage.us, down from 961,000 at 7:30 p.m. ET.

items: Macy's Thanksgiving Parade postponed to Saturday due to expected high winds
Flooding triggers evacuation order for dozens of properties on Vancouver Island

blocks.text: The data included more than 207,000 outages in Pennsylvania, over 179,000 in New Jersey, 139,000 in Maryland,106,000 in Virginia, 100,000 in Missouri and more than 68,000 in New Yorkstate.
Waves crash over dunes and onto the boardwalk on Thursday in Bethany Beach, Delaware. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Wind gusts of 80-112 km/h were reported or forecast across parts of Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York, and coastal New England, according to the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS).

It said conditions would gradually improve across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the heaviest rain and strongest winds moved into New England, although blustery conditions with gusts of 40 to 55 km/h were expected across parts of the East Coast on Friday.
New York City Emergency Management reported winds intensified on Thursday afternoon, reaching 90 km/h at LaGuardia Airport.

items: FedEx airplane overruns runway at Miami airport, temporarily closing all but 1 runway
Up to 9 hours of freezing rain in forecast for N.B., warning says

blocks.text: The NWS said strong onshore winds associated with the storm, combined with king tides, were causing coastal flooding in low-lying communities along portions of the East Coast.

Officials had already postponed Thursday's 100th edition of the annual Macy's ​Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City because of the storm threat, the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.

Separately on Thursday, President Donald Trump said he had approved about $100 million US in federal aid to Florida following severe storms and flooding there. He said the total included funding previously approved in connection with Hurricane Isaias.

articles.title: The coral reef watchers saving our ocean
articles.summary: Filipino marine scientists and volunteer divers work together to keep an eye on coral reefs — a collective pursuit in protecting the country's marine environment

blocks.text: BATANGAS, Philippines – In front of a house along the mangrove coast in Calatagan, Batangas, rafts and boats sat moored.

Jessie delos Reyes, 50, a slight-framed man who has lived in this house all his life, calls these rafts his floating classrooms; for more than half his life, he has dived in and out of the waters of the marine reserve just a few minutes away from his house.
He is known as Kuya Jessie of the floating houses in Calatagan. His name is familiar to locals, tourists, students, and marine scientists who come here for fieldwork and retreat.

The weather was fair that Tuesday morning in November. I joined Jessie on one of his dives to check the corals in Buntong Gasang, a coral monitoring site. The spot is a few minutes off the coast and not that deep. Buntong Gasang is adjacent to the Verde Island Passage, the famous waterway at the heart of the world’s Coral Triangle.
We used the floating classroom to go to Buntong Gasang. A motorized boat pulled the raft from the coast.

Three more divers made up Jessie’s team that morning — men who make a living teaching water safety skills, divers for nongovernmental organizations. That Tuesday, they were all volunteer divers for Calatagan Reef Patrollers or Carepas, which Jessie founded in 2004.

On the floating classroom, they moved at ease with their scuba diving equipment. On the table was a green thermos filled to the brim with kapeng barako (barako coffee) and bread for a quick breakfast.

They used a laminated coral health chart — composed of several shades of coral colors — from Australia’s University of Queensland. Divers hold this chart against the corals to compare colors and grade them properly.

When it turns 1 — or the palest shade of each color — it means the coral has bleached. Once they’ve identified the right shade of the coral with the chart, they write the grade on their slates. They submit these reports to authorities and experts.

During the dive, Jessie delegated tasks to the team. The safety diver entered the water first to check the current. Jessie laid the transect and collected data, with another diver tailing him to assist. Then another diver took photos and videos.
About 30 minutes later, after surfacing from the water, Jessie said there was good news and bad news. The good news: some of the corals that were bleaching a month ago showed signs of recovery.
“But the bad news is most of them were recently killed,” Jessie said after the dive. “There’s algae already. They were not able to recover.”

After many years of monitoring the corals in Calatagan, Jessie has become an advocate for “citizen science,” where community members work alongside scientists to monitor changes in the marine environment.
“The marine biologists, marine scientists, come and go,” Jessie said. “The community, even when their eyes are closed, even when they’re asleep, they know what’s happening in the community.”

blocks.caption: TRANSECT. Jessie delos Reyes holding a transect tape aboard the floating classroom while on the way to the coral monitoring site. Photo by Franz Lopez/Rappler

blocks.text: Coral scientist Wilfredo Licuanan has always dreamed of municipal fisherfolk checking the health of corals and reefs all on their own.

Licuanan, called Al by family and colleagues, is a De La Salle University professor who specializes in coral reefs. He established the SHORE Center, La Salle’s research center that pioneered a citizen science program on coral reef monitoring.

Al, 63, grew up in Diliman, Quezon City — the third generation in their family to study at University of the Philippines (UP). He took up marine science as an undergraduate, only learning to swim the summer before his first semester, before later shifting to zoology.

At the former Marine Science Center (now Marine Science Institute) at UP, he was a research assistant to the inimitable Edgardo Gomez, the center’s founding director. He eventually left the center and joined the La Salle faculty in 1997.

The next year, he started to manage the university’s Br. Alfred Shields FSC Marine Station in Lian, Batangas. The marine station lies in the western part of Lian, facing the Verde Island Passage and the West Philippine Sea. Its location is accessible to divers in the province, including volunteers from neighboring Calatagan.
Al said he has spent most of his time at the marine station as much as he could. Back then, it was still plain and bare, built like a bunkhouse along the coast in the remote part of town.

From 2014 to 2017, Al and his team at La Salle’s marine center surveyed reefs for a national assessment. The sheer scale of the work led them to develop further methods non-scientists could also use to assess coral communities and local reefs.

This eventually became the Alwan method. Alwan, a Tagalog word meaning “to ease,” evolved from the work of local and foreign researchers: an individual is trained to identify butterflyfish and target marine invertebrates and corals at a selected survey station.

By the end of the program, trainees are expected to know how to safely conduct a survey on their own, identify target species to determine reef health, and monitor bleaching triggered by climate change.

blocks.caption: TRAINER. Wilfredo Licuanan stands on the bow as water safety training starts in waters off the coast of Lian, Batangas. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

blocks.text: Forty years ago, when Al started his coral studies, he did not deliberately set out to promote citizen science.

There are not enough scientists, and it would be impossible to regularly check on reef health without the help of people who are most frequently at sea: the fishermen, sea patrol, locals, lifeguards, and even recreational divers.

“Those methods were actually an early form of citizen science in the sense that they were developed in Australia so that people who can dive but do not necessarily have the science training [can] do surveys in the Great Barrier Reef,” Al said.

A few weeks after my Calatagan visit with Jessie’s team, I joined Al and his SHORE Center staff in La Salle’s marine station in Lian. They had started training people from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) on how to monitor reefs.

It was another Tuesday morning at sea. The water was cold, and I was swimming toward the reef crest in front of the marine station, following Al toward a jutting rock. He moved deftly in the familiar waters, while I tried to keep up.

As we swam, the seafloor visible beneath me started to fade, and all I could see was blue. A few moments later, a blanket of dead staghorn corals appeared. I knew they were dead because of the fuzzy texture. Algae had grown and taken over.
Above water, Al told me that amid the dead staghorn corals, there were new, living ones.
“I’ll point them to you,” he told me. We swam a bit more, and the live staghorn corals were hard to miss. Staghorn corals have branches, and these had white tips.

Al later told me that meant they were still growing. I asked him how there could be living ones among the dead. It’s the current, Al said. Corals may be spawning in another part of the reef, or in another reef altogether, and the coral eggs and sperm made it to the area due to the current.

blocks.caption: SLATE. A diver takes note of target fish species on their slate. Photo from SHORE Center

blocks.text: A few minutes later, the BFAR staff who just finished water safety drills caught up with us at the reef. This was the first session of SHORE’s training for the BFAR. Among this session’s participants were the Carepas volunteer divers I visited in Calatagan weeks before.

Through the coral reef assessment from 2014 to 2017, Al and his team found a “marked decline” in the condition of local reefs in the past four decades (since the first assessment was conducted from 1976 to 1981).

Many of their assessment stations were in Luzon, specifically in the Verde Island Passage. The marked decline in conditions led the team to report then that “the establishment of marine protected areas, and other interventions in the past 40 years have not caused an appreciable impact on overall reef condition in general, except in particular localities.”
“Mostly, it’s climate change,” Al said in an interview before their fieldwork in Lian.
“I keep saying it’s the most visible manifestation of climate change,” he added. “Because when the water is hot, that is not a localized event. It happens in large sections of the sea.”

blocks.caption: LEARNING. A research assistant from SHORE (right) helps a BFAR staff with her fins before the water safety training starts. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

blocks.text: The world is already on track to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius limit that countries set to avoid the extreme impacts of climate change. At this point, drastic steps should already be taken to cut down greenhouse gas emissions.

Maintaining ocean health by protecting coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrasses can help cut down emissions. Australia and Turkey, co-presidents of this year’s largest climate summit, put the ocean at the heart of the conference, yet the talks broke down after a final draft deal failed to mention fossil fuels.
Back in Calatagan, the coast opposite Jessie’s house was lined with mangroves.
“We planted those mangroves on September 2, 2002,” he told me after that morning’s coral monitoring session. “We have mangroves, we have seagrass, we have corals. The ecosystem here is complete.”

Jessie grew up in Calatagan. His parents fished for a living, and Jessie himself was a fisherman before he became part of the sea patrol, became a lifeguard, learned to dive, and eventually founded his volunteer divers’ group.

blocks.caption: AFLOAT. The floating classrooms anchored in front of Jessie delos Reyes’ house in Calatagan, Batangas. Photo by Franz Lopez/Rappler
UNDERWATER. Jessie delos Reyes conducting coral assessment on November 3, 2026, in Calatagan, Batangas. Photo from Carepas

blocks.text: More than two decades ago, he attended a course that Al used to teach: marine biology for non-biologists. (“I taught it on the weekends,” Al told me in a separate interview. “Jessie was in the class.”)
Jessie has already seen it all: corals bleaching and recovering, the devastating impact of El Niño events in recent history, and typhoons that wreak havoc underwater.

His desire to protect the ocean is something he may have inherited from his parents, Jessie said — from fisherfolk who were at sea every day and who saw what a healthy ocean looked like and what it could give them. – Rappler.com
Quotes translated to English for brevity.
This story was produced with the support of Informed Earth as part of the COP31 Ocean Virtual Reporting Fellowship.

articles.title: SM Nuvali brings a new flagship mall – and traffic – to Laguna
articles.summary: SM's 91st mall distinguishes itself with an indoor garden inspired by Singapore's Gardens by the Bay

blocks.text: 91st MALL. SM Nuvali in Santa Rosa City, Laguna on November 26, 2026, with its unfinished office tower in the background
Rappler
SM's 91st mall distinguishes itself with an indoor garden inspired by Singapore's Gardens by the Bay

items: SM Nuvali, the largest mall in Laguna, officially opened on November 27, featuring a unique indoor garden and a focus on sustainability.

The mall includes various amenities such as a community library, multiple cinemas including the country's first LED cinema screens, and a curated selection of restaurants, some of which are new to the area.
Despite its grand opening, traffic congestion has already been a concern, prompting SM to coordinate with local authorities to manage traffic flow and minimize congestion for visitors.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
LAGUNA, Philippines – SM has built quite a mall in the south – its biggest in Laguna, to be exact.
SM Nuvali, which officially opened its doors to the public on Friday, November 27, is a spectacle. At 190,525 square meters, it’s SM Prime’s 91st mall and the fifth in the province alone.

But this flagship mall stands apart with its sprawling air-conditioned indoor garden and a glass-paned roof to let some sunlight stream in. On the floors above, restaurants and cafés overlook the patches of green, with playgrounds and a Paw Park.

“SM Nuvali is different because it brings together nature, sustainability, and thoughtfully curated retail experiences in one destination,” SM Supermalls president Steven Tan told Rappler. “At its heart is a garden within the mall, offering an outdoor-inspired environment that is air-conditioned and designed for comfort, while being LEED-certified.”

blocks.caption: SM Nuvali opening
SM Nuvali opening
GARDEN. An indoor garden is the centerpiece of SM Nuvali. Photos by Leanne Jazul/Rappler

blocks.text: There’s a grand staircase, a community library called Book Nook with more than 10,000 books, and, on the top floor, a chapel.
Moviegoers can look forward to four regular cinemas, an IMAX auditorium with its own “IMAX Pods,” and two Director’s Club cinemas equipped with what SM calls the country’s first LED cinema screens.

blocks.caption: MOVIE. SM Nuvali features the country’s first LED cinema screens. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

blocks.text: And though it’s new, it’s far from empty. If you’re going for food, you’ll find all the usual suspects, which Tan told Rappler was “carefully curated” – Din Tai Fung, Wildflour, Hoshino Coffee, among others – but some are showing up in Laguna for the first time, like Michelin Bib Gourmand awardee Some Thai, Golden Yolk, George & Onnie’s, and The Matcha Tokyo.
Tucked in the Food Hall is SM’s Game Park, where you can squeeze in a round of billiards or arcade games between meals.

blocks.caption: MEALS. SM Nuvali brings Makati’s Scratch smashburgers down south. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

blocks.text: “Here, we can come together, enjoy a meal, and tell each other stories of our lives and our love,” Tan said at the mall’s opening gala on Thursday night, November 26. “We need community more than ever.”

Tan credited the Sy family “for their vision and passion to bring this development to the next level,” and then called SM Prime president Jeffrey Lim and Hans “Chico” Sy Jr. – son of Hans Sy and president of engineering, design, and development – to the stage.

blocks.caption: CHEERS! (Left to right) Hans Sy Jr., Steven Tan, and Jeffrey Lim offer a toast during the opening of SM Nuvali. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

blocks.text: In the crowd too was Chico’s sister Hanna Carinna Sy, senior assistant vice president for marketing and leasing. The third-generation Sys are now helping to design the malls, giving the newer ones a touch of youth. And of course there was Hans Sy, who looked on like the proud father that he was. (READ: SM Harrison Plaza opening by end-2027 with entire floor for Gen Z)

“I cannot tell you enough how excited we are to welcome people to a brand new home in the South. But that will be for tomorrow,” Tan said. “So tonight, we hold this moment to ourselves and celebrate!”

blocks.caption: TYCOON. SM Prime executive committee chairman Hans Sy poses during SM Nuvali’s opening night gala. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

blocks.text: Tomorrow, of course, means cars, and probably lots of them.

Even before the mall officially opened, motorists and residents had already been complaining online about worsening traffic along the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay Road, particularly around the traffic lights in front of the mall.

SM Nuvali sits right at the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay exit of the Cavite-Laguna Expressway (CALAX), mixing mallgoers with motorists entering and leaving the expressway. With the height of Christmas shopping season approaching, congestion could worsen even for motorists who simply use the expressway to get home or travel to Tagaytay.

Asked about the traffic situation, Tan told Rappler in a message: “We recognize the importance of managing traffic, especially with the area’s continued growth. SM Nuvali is coordinating closely with the relevant local government units and traffic authorities to support traffic management measures, including proper vehicle ingress and egress, traffic flow management, and coordination during peak hours to help minimize congestion and ensure a smoother experience for motorists and visitors.”
When Rappler visited the mall on Thursday, traffic had partly backed up to near the CALAX exit. That was before the general public could even enter the mall. – Rappler.com
