articles.title: DOH hospitals have 150% bed occupancy; 10,000 health workers needed
articles.summary: Hospitals of the Department of Health (DOH) are overcrowded at 150% bed occupancy rate following the implementation of the zero balance billing policy, with 10,000 healthcare worker positions still…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 5:06pm

Hospitals of the Department of Health (DOH) are overcrowded at 150% bed occupancy rate following the implementation of the zero balance billing policy, with 10,000 healthcare worker positions still vacant at these facilities.

During the interpellation of the DOH's budget at the plenary session on Friday, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto asked how much the zero balance billing policy also raised the number of patients at DOH hospitals.
The DOH, through its budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito, affirmed that there was an increase.

"For zero balance billing, the ones that availed of the zero balance billing programs in DOH hospitals is about 4.2 million patients," Ejercito said regarding the government health policy which seeks to remove out-of-pocket expenses of Filipinos for health services.

Ejercito added that there were also 400 beneficiaries for zero balance billing in local government unit (LGU) hospitals during the fourth quarter of the year. The number was low since the establishment of zero balance billing in LGU hospitals was recent.
EXPLAINER: Zero Balance Billing, No Co-Payment Policy — What they mean for patients

Under the zero balance billing policy, PhilHealth members confined in ward or basic accommodations are not required to pay out-of-pocket expenses for medical services covered by their PhilHealth benefits.
Procedures, operations, and medicines covered by PhilHealth should also be provided without additional charges in wards of basic rooms.
All PhilHealth members, regardless of socioeconomic status, are eligible to avail of zero balance billing.
Crowded hospitals
Asked about the bed occupancy rate, Ejercito said "on the average or 'yung mga estimate po talaga mga 150% (on the average or the estimate, it is really 150%.)"

Ejercito said the DOH was seeking the Senate’ help to better capacitate provincial and LGU hospitals to help decongest the DOH hospitals. Private hospitals are also being engaged to allot 10% for their beds for zero balance billing.
Later on, Sotto said many doctors, nurses and health care workers leave for jobs abroad. He asked how many positions in DOH hospitals are unfilled because of the workers who leave.
“Ang unfilled positions talaga for healthcare workers, kasama na po 'yung nurses and others, for DOH hospitals mga 10,000 na ang kailangan,” Ejercito said.
(The unfilled positions for healthcare workers, including the nurses and others, for DOH hospitals, there are around 10,000 needed.)

To alleviate this, Ejercito said that the DOH had a ladderized program to allow healthcare workers to get promoted and improve their positions. The agency was also talking with state universities and colleges to have more healthcare scholarships so that there is a tie-in agreement to return service. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte says resignation 'out of the question' amid impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 5:01pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.
“No, sir. Resignation, that is out of the question. I already answered that several times during the course of the trial,” Duterte said in a press conference.

“It is something that I cannot do because I feel that it's a betrayal of the 32.2 million people who voted for me, and of course the general public, if I resign from the position of Vice President,” she added.

Vice President Sara Duterte reiterates she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial: “That’s out of the question…that’s something I cannot do because it’s betrayal to the public.” @gmanews https://t.co/0cqfTRpPmp Other Stories — Giselle Ombay (@giselleombay_) November 27, 2026
The Vice President is currently facing an impeachment trial before the Senate impeachment court.

Her defense team has been presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case, alleging her unexplained wealth due to her supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as constitutionally required for the President and Vice President.
Preparing for worst
Duterte also admitted that she and her defense team are always “preparing for the worst” now that the trial is nearing its end and the Senate impeachment court is expected to issue a verdict soon.

“Because if there's an acquittal, it will just be a continuation of what we are doing now for the Office of the Vice President. So next year, all the projects and all the programs will be implemented as if it's 2026 or 2025 or 2024—a matter of difference of budget,” she explained.
“But if it's a verdict of guilty, it will come with a lot of consequences,” she added.
The Vice President said her primary concern, if she is ever convicted in her impeachment trial, is the expected loss of employment in the OVP.
She said around 300 families of employees from various OVP satellite offices across the country may be affected by the possible conviction.
“Because the satellite offices are coterminous to me as Vice President. So that is our first worry, the jobs of those OVP employees who are coterminous,” she said.
Duterte also said she is preparing to ask those stationed in the OVP headquarters in Mandaluyong City to move out if she gets convicted.
“So those are the things that we need to prepare for. But if it's a verdict of acquittal, then we don't have to prepare for anything except for the rollout of projects for 2027,” she said.
Acceptance
Nevertheless, Duterte said she will accept whatever the decision will be at the end of the trial—whether she will get acquitted or convicted.

“We will accept whatever it is that the judgment of the Senate impeachment court will give for the impeachment trial, and we will all have to live with the consequences of this out-of-mind decision of President Marcos,” she said.
Malacañang has repeatedly said that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is not influencing the impeachment proceedings against the Vice President.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Jays tickets, drums and Tinder: Hundreds of purchases made with Toronto city credit cards raise questions about misuse
articles.summary: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by…

image.caption: An analysis of City of Toronto credit card expenditure data by CBC News has found that city staff spent thousands of dollars on purchases that appear questionable. (Yulia Grigoryeva/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by CBC News has found.

The transactions are documented in a list of expense records made publicly available by the City of Toronto. They detail the spending habits of 88 city divisions through their use of city-issued credit cards, also known as purchasing cards or PCards.

While meant to ease bottlenecks for low-dollar purchases like office supplies, a snapshot of recorded expenses analyzed by CBC News found some transactions appeared questionable, with several legal, financial and policy experts saying the PCard program requires better oversight.
CBC News shared its findings with the city and Mayor Olivia Chow's office, alongside a list of extensive questions about the PCard program.
Chow's office did not acknowledge the request for comment or respond to an interview request. The city did not respond to an interview request.

items: Toronto to look at 3 new revenue tools as city faces budget pressures
Toronto's top bureaucrat leaving city hall. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Mark Rozic, the city's director of accounting services, said in a statement that while PCard transaction data is publicly available, it "does not tell the full story of what was purchased, why it was needed, or the city service or activity it supported."
CBC News did ask the city to provide supporting documentation to help explain transactions that appeared questionable, which the city did not provide.
Instead, Rozic said the PCard program has "multiple layers of oversight" that include spending limits and restrictions, mandatory training and management review.

"The City takes its stewardship of public funds seriously and expects all cardholders and approvers to use City purchasing cards responsibly, transparently and in accordance with program requirements,” he said.
The findings come as the city grapples with its financial outlook and looks to find additional revenue tools to support its books.

CBC News also reached out to CUPE 79 for comment, a local union branch whose members include City of Toronto workers. Spokesperson Tor Sandberg said in a statement Thursday that the union can't provide comment because it's unclear whether the PCard purchases in question were made by management or the front-line staff it represents.
How Toronto's new revenue ideas could hit your wallet
How we tracked this information and what we found

The city's PCard data has over 800,000 entries, with expenditures for several city divisions going back over a decade. Not every division had updated transaction records or records that went back that far.

CBC News picked eight city divisions and conducted a line-by-line review of their transactions. Transactions that appeared questionable were then put into a spreadsheet that was shared with experts, Toronto's auditor general, the city and the mayor's office.
The spreadsheet included purchases from the following city divisions:

items: Seniors and long-term care: $1,986 for Blue Jays tickets bought in 2026.
Toronto Water: $169.50 spent on "other expenses" at Coach in 2023.
Toronto paramedics: $1,283.34 for drums bought at Long and McQuade in 2025.
City clerks: $146.89 for a "world deluxe subscription" with Ancestry.ca in 2025.
Environment: $100 for a "presentation of appreciation item" bought at Body Blitz, a downtown spa, in 2023.

blocks.text: "On the surface … this is weird," said Zac Spicer, an associate professor at York University's school of public policy, who reviewed a snapshot of the recorded expenses for CBC News.

"This is public money there. The [city] should be willing to sort of justify what is happening here," he said, noting that while PCards are meant to ease administrative burdens, they don't mean "unchecked spending."

Among the expenses analyzed by CBC News, thousands do appear to check out: $196.56 paid by Toronto 311 for an order of office binders, $451.32 worth of soccer balls bought by the FIFA secretariat for the city's Soccer For All mini pitches, $85.03 for screws, ceiling tiles and plywood bought by Toronto Water.
Some also appear to be disputed, including a total of $249.95 spent on Tinder by Toronto Water in 2016.
Thousands of PCard expenditures do appear to check out, such as purchases made for building supplies by Toronto Water and soccer balls by Toronto's FIFA secretariat. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
City did not provide PCard policy
CBC News asked the City of Toronto for a document that outlined its PCard spending policies. The city did not provide one. No public document outlining how the city uses the cards was found.

In an emailed statement, Frédérique Mazerolle, spokesperson for the city, said the program provides city divisions with a "convenient and cost-effective way to make certain purchases on behalf of the city."

Mazerolle said each PCard has set transaction and monthly spending limits as well as restrictions on the types of purchases that can be made. Only certain city staff get authorization to use the cards, she said.

Eligible PCard expenses are those needed for city business and permitted by its purchasing rules, such as certain office supplies, subscriptions, pre-authorized business travel and emergency purchases, Mazerolle said.
Many divisions recorded all-time spending highs
Paul Emanuelli, a procurement lawyer in Toronto with knowledge of the PCard system, said some of the expenditures identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city.
"Many of these expenditures, they're really hard, on the surface, to really explain what they're for," he said.
Paul Emanuelli, a Toronto procurement lawyer, says some of the PCard transactions identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city. (Paul Borkwood/CBC)
Several city divisions had their annual PCard spending reach over $1 million. Divisions with some of the highest PCard expenditures for a single recorded year included:

items: Parks and recreation: $10 million spent in 2025.
Water: $3.43 million spent in 2025.
Seniors and long-term care: $1.89 million spent in 2026.
Shelter and support: $1.36 million spent in 2025.

blocks.text: If the transactions are publicly listed online, they should be able to stand on their own and be "self-evident," Emanuelli said.
"In procurement, one of the foundational concepts is transparency, because it's public expenditure. A fragmented disclosure is not useful."
Mayor Olivia Chow lays out vision for new term in 1st council meeting
Auditor general should review: forensic accountant
CBC News identified 44 of the 88 city divisions had PCard spending reach an all-time high this year, or for their latest reported full year.
Some divisions, like environment, have had spending reach an all-time high in 2026, despite the year not being over yet.
Some divisions are also using the cards more than ever, with the number of transactions increasing for 40 out of the 88 divisions in 2026 or their latest reported full year, according to the data.

Charles Smedmor, a forensic accountant who's previously worked with former Toronto Auditor General Jeff Griffiths, said the expenses identified by CBC News warrant a closer review by city council or the current auditor general, Tara Anderson.
"Looking at it, some [expenses] are red flags, some are orange flags, some are reasonable," he said.
"These sorts of things have to be followed up."
Smedmor said the city should provide supporting documents related to each expense in order to get a clearer sense of what transactions can be deemed reasonable.

items: Mayor Chow points to city's fiscal challenges in first meeting of new Toronto council

blocks.text: City auditor general recommended increasing PCard use

From a procurement standpoint, Emanuelli said he was "pleasantly surprised" to see many of the city's PCard expenditures appeared well documented and justifiable. But the expenses that appeared inappropriate are still a "serious matter," especially if the PCard program continues to expand, something the city's auditor general recommended last year.

It's not the first time this recommendation has been made. In 2009, the auditor general also recommended the city expand its PCard program, with the caveat that it also improve PCard training, overall policy, and safeguards.
City council adopted the recommendation in 2010, but Anderson's 2025 audit notes it has "remained open for more than 15 years."
Toronto pauses most hiring due to financial pressures
The audit's executive summary said staff and management voiced concerns PCard rules limited "operational efficiency," and they recommended their use be increased, according to the audit.

At the same time, the audit acknowledged there was minimal data available to figure out where bottlenecks were happening. It recommended the city consider expanding PCard use anyway, so long as additional resources were provided on how to appropriately use the cards, such as refresher training each year.

items: AG report reveals city parks workers spending less time working than they say they are
City staff stealing packages, working other jobs on sick leave: What Toronto's auditor uncovered in 2025

blocks.text: Alexandra Galanis, spokesperson for the auditor general, said the office cannot comment on the expenditure data shared by CBC News because it would need to review additional "contextual information and supporting documents" from city divisions.
She said every city division is responsible for "line-by-line" reviews of PCard expenditures, and authorizing managers "must ensure proper oversight of PCard use within their division."
"Our office takes matters related to misuse of funds seriously," Galanis said in an emailed statement.
Galanis also acknowledged the recommendation to expand PCard use has been open for over a decade, but it's the only recommendation — out of 20 made in 2009 — that remains open.

articles.title: 2,000 wild species live in our homes with us, study finds
articles.summary: You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. If you find them, here's why scientists say you shouldn't take them outside.

image.caption: The bold jumping spider was one of the spiders commonly found in people's homes and submitted to the Never Home Alone study, to researchers' surprise. (Catherine Scott)

blocks.text: Science·Updated
You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. If you find them, here's why scientists say you shouldn't take them outside.
Never Home Alone citizen science study uncovers ecosystems in our buildings

You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. And if you find them, scientists say there are reasons why you shouldn't put them outside.

Homes in Canada and the U.S. are inhabited not just by humans and their pets but by at least 2,000 other species, from Asian lady beetles to a huge diversity of spiders to the occasional alligator, reports the study published this week in Ecology.
Bradley Allf, the Colorado State University ecologist who led the study, said the findings showcase "the ways in which we're not so separate from nature despite the many ways we try to wall it out."
Allf said his goal was to treat the indoors like the savannah or rainforest and get a sense of what the ecosystem looks like in the relatively new but growing habitat created by humans.
There's already evidence that it's full of ecological mysteries "right under our nose that we don't know very much about."

This green anole was submitted to the Never Home Alone project from a home in Raleigh, N.C. That was among the species that lead research Bradley Allf contributed to the project. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)
How science got inside so many people's homes

Allf and his team didn't explore people's homes, as scientists had in a previous study. Instead, they launched a citizen science (also known as community science) project called Never Home Alone on the iNaturalist app. It invited ordinary people to send photos of wild species they found indoors. Those species were then identified by a team of experts.
The Great Wild Indoors – Insects Hiding in Your Home

The project received more than 23,000 photos from 3,000 people in every U.S. state and every Canadian province (though not all territories) between 1996 and 2024. Most were from homes, but some were also from offices, schools, airports and other buildings.

And while experts were able to identify more than 2,000 species, the researchers believe there were more, since nearly half the observations could only be identified as belonging to a more general grouping (such as combfoot spiders), rather than as individual species. About 52 per cent of species were observed only once.
The most common species in our homes (besides us)
The most commonly recorded species in the study did include some pests, as expected. The varied carpet beetle, which can damage carpets, furniture and clothing, was No. 4, for example.
But No. 1 was the Asian lady beetle, which came as a surprise to Allf.
"We know almost nothing about what they're doing inside," he said. "And yet, they're found in hundreds of homes across the U.S. and Canada."
(CBC)
Catherine Scott is an arachnologist from Memorial University in St. John's who co-authored the study and identified many of the spiders.
"I was surprised by the diversity of spiders found indoors," she said.

While there were lots of expected species such as cellar spiders (the long-bodied cellar spider was the fifth most common in the study) and false black widows, which spin cobwebs, the bold jumping spider was also frequently reported.
"They're big and flashy and not particularly known as a house spider," she said.
But Scott noted that the most commonly reported species aren't necessarily the most common, as people tend to notice larger, more brightly coloured things that move around more.
Allf said the fact that spiders, which are predators, are so common is evidence that indoor spaces are "a real ecosystem … where species are eating one another or where there's food webs."

This is one of the most recent observations from the Never Home Alone project. Submitted from Fort George, B.C., it's been tentatively identified as a hobo spider. Spiders were among the most common types of animals found, and there was a huge diversity. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)

But he said there are lots of questions about how creatures live and interact within that ecosystem, including cellar spiders: "How often do they eat? How do they meet other cellar spiders and reproduce?"
He hopes studies like this will begin to help answer such questions.
Why you shouldn't put them outside
Allf acknowledged that many people's gut reaction when encountering other species in their homes is to squish them or take them outside.
But in fact, for many species, the indoors is their natural habitat. They're adapted to the controlled climate and food resources and are more protected from predators there.
"If they go outside, it might be a more dangerous place for them," Allf said.
This Asian lady beetle was submitted to the project from Longeuil, Que. This was the species most commonly submitted to the project in North America. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)
He gave the example of German cockroaches, a species he said has never been found outdoors.
"I think there's probably many more species like that that we just don't know about yet."
Allf suggested that when people find an organism from another species in their home, they should consider whether it's dangerous or bothering them.
"If the answers to those questions are no, then maybe just leave it there."
Scott noted that spiders are in people's homes for a reason.
"They're doing their job eating insects," she said. "They're natural pest control and they don't want to bother you, so try to coexist."
What citizen science can do

Jeremy Kerr is a University of Ottawa ecologist who has developed and used citizen science apps extensively in his research on butterflies and bees, but wasn't involved in the Never Home Alone project.
He said he loves the name and the concept and suggested it might make people feel more connected to nature and appreciate its value.
"I think there's something to be gained by simply recognizing that nature is everywhere, and maybe by extension, it's worth being curious about it," he said.

So far, he said, this is a very small citizen science database compared with larger ones containing hundreds of thousands to billions of observations that allow researchers to answer detailed questions about species such as birds. More observations about indoor ecosystems would be valuable, he said, providing a better idea of the dominant species in different regions, for example.
In fact, the Never Home Alone project is ongoing and accepting observations from around the world.
Scott hopes the publication of this study will encourage more people to contribute.

articles.title: Danielle Smith’s hold over UCP takes centre stage as 7,000 members registered for annual meeting
articles.summary: Alberta's United Conservatives kick off their fifth annual general meeting under Premier Danielle Smith Friday, a gathering expected to reveal much about the party’s future a little more than a month…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to party faithful at a prior United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary in 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary

Alberta's United Conservatives kick off their fifth annual general meeting under Premier Danielle Smith Friday, a gathering expected to reveal much about the party’s future a little more than a month after a divisive referendum.
Annual gathering to draw party faithful (and those in crisis of faith)
In the days after the vote, Smith said the UCP would not be turned into a vehicle for independence.
But party unity remains elusive.
Several constituency association presidents have refused to sign pledges backing the results, meaning the independence issue remains a live one heading into the weekend.
Smith herself has advocated for conservatives to band together, suggesting she expects a “really robust [and] fun” debate at the annual meeting.

“We sadly always seem to try to find the things that blow us apart. I keep on wanting to try to find the things that will draw us together,” Smith told longtime separatist Cory Morgan in a recent interview.
Some attendees, though, expect these fissures to come into public view on the convention floor over the course of the weekend.
“I think she’s going to get absolutely surprised at the AGM,” said Martin Belanger, a social media influencer who has been a vocal proponent for Alberta independence on his channel, Martyupnorth.

“If people think that Jeff Rath getting up in front of the mic last year and saying, ‘Who here is pro-independence?’ [was notable] … You’re going to get a moment like that, after moment, after moment.”

Jeffrey Rath, co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, speaks at a referendum watch party in October. At last year’s AGM, Rath received a standing ovation at a microphone after challenging Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)
For Belanger and others in his camp, frustration lies with Smith’s approach to Ottawa.
“Some people are fed up with negotiations,” Belanger said.

“In this big tent, we have different paths, and she’s trying to shove us down one path. I don’t think she’s genuine when she says she wants that discussion, because some of her actions of late don’t reflect that.”
Remarks expected from 3 conservative premiers
More than 7,000 members have registered for the event at Calgary’s BMO Centre. On Friday, candidates for the UCP board will deliver speeches.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson are expected to deliver remarks later in the day.

British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson looks on during the swearing-in ceremony at Government House in Victoria on Nov. 20. Doerkson and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe are expected to deliver remarks on Friday at the 2026 United Conservative Party annual general meeting. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
During the event, members will vote for eight people to join the party’s board while also voting on proposed policy matters. Smith will deliver a keynote address Saturday morning.

It will be a balancing act for Smith as she is tasked with appearing as though she has a reasonably united party behind her, without conceding too much ground to the separatists in the party, said Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary.

“I would imagine that there’s a substantial number of party members who are sympathetic to the idea that they have to set aside their differences, because this is the last convention going into an election,” Young said.
“What proportion of the members those are … it’s anyone’s guess, really.”
Resolutions on land acknowledgements, washrooms
Members will also vote on a series of grassroots policy resolutions during the meeting. While non-binding, they signal the desires of party faithful and have influenced party legislation in the past.
For instance, at last year’s annual general meeting, Smith pointed to recent legislation that she said was inspired by the “attack” on psychologist and media personality Jordan Peterson.
“That came from you. That was your policy last AGM. We're calling it the 'Peterson law,’” Smith said during her speech to delegates.
As she has at AGMs past, Smith will hold an “accountability session” in front of members on Saturday.
Delegates cast their votes at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary on Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
This year, delegates will debate policy resolutions that will be voted on by members during the convention, including:

items: Ending the use of land acknowledgements by the government, as well as all publicly-funded institutions and entities.
Adopting policy that would “protect the safety and privacy of women and girls in schools and public facilities,” including washrooms and change areas.
Mandate that Alberta use "all available legal avenues” to challenge federal land claims, including Indigenous claims that "may infringe on private property owners and their rights."
Pass legislation that would require an MLA who departs their party to sit as an independent member and seek a renewed mandate from voters before joining another party.

blocks.text: Notably, there are no policy resolutions tied to the notion of separating from Canada to be debated.

Near the site of the convention, some people opposed to the UCP government's priorities have promised to hold a sort of “accountability” session of their own, saying there will be “costumes, signs, music” and other forms of protest.
“There are so many awful issues!” the Calgary Raging Grannies wrote in a post on Facebook.
Who will sit on the party's board?
To many, the biggest thing to watch over the weekend will be the results of the board elections. Half of the provincial board is elected each year, with winners going on to serve two years.

Going into the next election, this group will set the rules and the processes for nomination and platform development, making this key to the party’s future, said Colin Aitchison, managing director of western Canada with Enterprise Canada.

“I think a lot of the party membership … they want the party to be best positioned to beat the NDP and Naheed Nenshi in the next election,” said Aitchison, who was a former spokesperson for the UCP under ministers Adriana LaGrange and Nicholas Milliken.
“In order to do that, you need to have a unified leadership at the top, and one that supports the current leader and their agenda.”

items: The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention

blocks.text: Some running for the party board have dismissed the idea that the disagreements that have emerged over past months can be resolved simply by supporting a unity principle.
“A strong leader should welcome a board willing to speak candidly on behalf of its members,” wrote Vince Byfield, a board candidate, on his Substack.

“Sometimes that means offering support, sometimes it means proposing alternatives, and sometimes it means saying that members have serious concerns about a particular decision. None of those actions is inherently disloyal.”
Board election results are expected to be delivered on Saturday evening, just before the adjournment of the annual general meeting.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a senior writer with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Focker-In-Law isn't terrible. It's just a sitcom
articles.summary: Focker-In-Law is nothing compared to 2000's Meet the Parents. But if comparing to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic situation-comedy field the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself…

image.caption: This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows Ben Stiller, left, and Ariana Grande in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Universal Pictures/Paramount)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Focker-In-Law is nothing compared to 2000's Meet the Parents. But if comparing to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic situation-comedy field the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself in, it's ... fine? Mostly? Watchable, let's say. And that's all these things are going for.
Ben Stiller, Ariana Grande-led instalment of Meet the Parents franchise deliver middling, serviceable comedy
There is a fairly simple way to avoid seeing how far the mighty have fallen. Just avoid finding out where they fell from.

When it comes to the probably-too-cutely-titled Fockers franchise, that seems to be the recipe for success. Because following 2010's Little Fockers, 2004’s Meet the Fockers and finally, the normally titled comedy that started it all, 2000's Meet the Parents, there’s really only one way to avoid disappointment: Only watch the entries earning their buck off the punny name of our titular Gaylord (though he'd much prefer you call him Greg) Focker. Or skip them all and just stick to the seminal indie smash success whose title didn’t lean on him at all.

Clearly, some critics didn't take this advice when heading into Focker-In-Law, the newest iteration of the Ben Stiller-led comedy premise. So far holding the second-lowest Rotten Tomatoes score of the critically panned sequels, the film's dour reception appears to broadly circle the same complaints. Too broad. Too cliche. And — aside from the bubbly Focker-in-law herself, Ariana Grande — too dour. That means you, Ben Stiller.

That, though, is true only if you don't judge it on face value. Because really, what else did you expect? If it was for a return to the heights of Jay Roach's "original" — itself a sort-of remake of the 1992 comedy of the same name — you're out of luck. But if comparing it to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic, situation-comedy field that the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself in, it's ... fine? Mostly? Watchable, let's say. And that's all these things are going for.

Because more than 25 years after his famously awkward, increasingly idiotic protagonist turned a meeting with exacting father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) into a cavalcade of I Love Lucy-esque disasters of his own moronic making, Greg is left with few to no grounded choices. What else to do but what director/co-writer (and Zoolander co-writer) John Hamburg opted for here: a feud between overbearing Greg and his son (Skyler Gisondo) Henry's impossibly perfect, ex-hostage-negotiator girlfriend, Olivia (Grande)?

If you're waiting for some type of subversion, keep waiting. The central conflict — and its resolution — is about as hard to guess as what, exactly, Samuel L. Jackson is going to find in the cockpit in Snakes on a Plane.

Take it from Greg's long-suffering wife, Pam (Teri Polo), to whom director Hamburg even needs to give an expositional line about how Greg only acts this insane on family trips. (If not, why wouldn't she have divorced him yet?) Greg is now older than Jack was during the events of the first film. Wouldn't it be crazy if it were his turn to play the Jack to his own son's new flame?

Cue the most basic, least innovative evolution to allow this repeated framing to occur, once again. Greg is now the one to suggest strapping Olivia into the lie detector chair, to battle Olivia in a bizarrely high-stakes race by unsuspecting pedestrians (though this time on ludicrously slow bikes instead of sedans).

But there's one new complication thrown into the mix, in that all the while, he's still desperately and pathetically trying to earn the affections of his family — and of Jack, which he attempts with unsettling, pseudo-romantic passion.
This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows Ben Stiller, left, and Robert De Niro in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)
The solution

For high-concept features doomed by both their initial originality and unexpected success, there are few options to keep them rolling as a series. And, as Fockers' consistent box office success in the face of equally consistent negative reviews shows, there's one method that can keep at least the money rolling in: Become a sitcom.

That is, figure out a way to put your characters in the exact same situation with the near-exact same logline as before. For The Hangover, simply lose a different friend — or have him kidnapped this time. In Home Alone, perform a narrative reset by losing Kevin all over again. But have him lose his parents instead. And always: have every character constantly remark on how ridiculous it is this is all happening again, so the audience doesn't have to.

The sitcom format works for television, as the pilot is expected to showcase a formula to revisit later. But it's different for film, where the original is expected to be its own self-contained story. How do you have your character face the same problem again when previous entries had them surmount whatever central flaw brought the problem about in the first place?

items: Sunrise on the Reaping may be a prequel, but it's the worst way to start The Hunger Games
Club Kid is one of TIFF's best. It might make you cry

blocks.text: If you're Home Alone, it's simple: Just get a new kid for the (somehow) four sequels beyond Macaulay Culkin. For Focker-In-Law, the solution is even simpler: Have Greg revert to the same psychotically self-conscious behaviour he's exhibited in every film so far, despite the character development with which the previous films ostensibly all ended.

While Jack has long ago accepted him into his coveted "circle of trust," Focker-In-Law continues to set up hypothermia-inducing ice-plunges and pants-ripping dog attacks largely around Greg's obsessive need to continue impressing him.

And the rest of the cast is left as shallow supporting acts to gawk at the unbelievably short-sighted choices made by this grown man, who presumably has a 401(k) and a consistently paid mortgage, yet also just burned his eyebrows off after pouring nearly a full bottle of whisky onto a flaming pan.

There is the parallel plotline: Greg's competition with Olivia's funny — if, once again, one-dimensional — and powerful perfectionism. In fact, the only person who seems to have changed much is Jack. Previously a meat-eating traditionalist, this Jack is now, inexplicably, a vegan on a health kick who immediately takes to Olivia and Henry's relationship, arguing that sexually active couples should be allowed to share a room and even complimenting the gorgeous vegan meal she cooks as Greg's burnt steak smoulders untouched on the plate.

This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows, from left, Eduardo Franco, Beanie Feldstein, Teri Polo, Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)

This does work against Focker-In-Law's success in a vacuum. Where Greg's neuroses could be excused when he was up against an unbelievable monster, he becomes much harder to empathize with when up against normal humans. A doubly strange double-down: Stiller's protagonist genuinely becomes the least likeable player in his own movie.

Still, the undeniable unoriginality is not enough to make Focker-In-Law unwatchable. Greg's daughter's live-in boyfriend, Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), endears with the hilariously earnest patter he showed off in his criminally short turn in Stranger Things.

Then there is Grande's typical, unflappable comedic timing, which picks up the pace whenever things really start to drag. And there is the no longer novel yet ever-present formula, reheated and presented once more.
Again, it's nothing even close to the serviceable, interesting first entry, in a franchise that should probably now be sorted by pre- and post-Focker. But otherwise, it is … fine?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Small businesses worry potential consumer pullback could cut into critical holiday sales
articles.summary: The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could…

image.caption: As the busy holiday shopping season gets underway, small business owners are worried consumers might cut back on spending this year, denting their sales. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

blocks.text: Business

The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could dent their sales.
Pullback in spending biggest threat to holiday sales, according to survey of independent business owners
It's the most wonderful — and most important — time of the year for retailers like Kristi Wozniak: the holiday shopping season.
"It's very big," said Wozniak, owner and founder of Keylime Activewear in Sherwood Park, Alta. "We are in our busiest season right now for sure."
Wozniak says a quarter of her sales come from holiday shopping, with December being their busiest month.
But sales have been down recently compared to previous years, and she's worried that shoppers slowing their spending could cut into those critical holiday sales.
"Customers are definitely more cautious where they're spending their dollars," Wozniak said.
She's not alone. As small businesses struggle with tariffs and rising costs, some are worried that less spending by consumers this holiday season could deal another blow.
Kristi Wozniak, owner of Keylime Athletics, stands beside a sign advertising discounts at her storefront in Sherwood Park, Alta. (Submitted by Kristi Wozniak)

In a survey of 1,675 of its members from across the country, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business found that the holiday season is an important part of the financial outlook for four in 10 respondents. And 73 per cent of that group said a pullback in spending posed the biggest threat to holiday sales.

"In times of worsening affordability in the middle of a trade war, lack of consumer demand has actually been a key threat for many small businesses," said Ryan Mitton, the CFIB's director of legislative affairs for B.C.
And retail sales data from Statistics Canada shows consumers might, in fact, be trying to cut down on their spending.

Retail sales ticked up in September by 0.8 per cent — but that was driven mostly by a jump in how much consumers were spending at gas stations. And an early estimate for October forecasted a 1.5 per cent drop in retail sales.

items: Food and shelter have driven Canada's affordability crisis. Health care isn't far behind

blocks.text: Those figures give a "very weak kickoff point" for retail sales in the last quarter of the year, according to Michael Davenport, a senior economist with Oxford Economics.

He says high gas prices due to the war in Iran have been squeezing household budgets, while the weak job market and volatility in financial markets are weighing on consumer's confidence. And while consumer spending has been pretty resilient throughout the year despite some of those factors, he expects they'll cause Canadians to spend less in coming months.

items: Canadian economy lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7%

blocks.text: "All of these factors are kind of coming together, we think, to lead to a bit of a slowdown in consumer spending growth towards the end of 2026 and early 2027."
Black Friday deal hunting with AI? What chatbots can miss
If holiday sales do take a hit, Wozniak says it could leave her with less cash to order new stock in the new year and force her to cut back some hours for staff.
"[If] we didn't make enough money for the previous season, now we're looking for cashflow options," Wozniak said.
She's stopped purchasing from some of her U.S. suppliers due to tariffs and to keep down costs related to shipping and the unfavorable exchange rate between the Canadian and U.S. dollar.
But rising manufacturing costs have still shrunken her profit margins in recent years, meaning she can't offer massive Black Friday discounts on clothing at Keylime like big box stores can.

items: Can AI chatbots really help shoppers find the best deals?
You told us how you're keeping holiday costs down this year

blocks.text: Despite that, she's offering deals on gift cards and discounts that scale with the number of items shoppers buy, which she hopes will be enough to get buyers through the door — and spending some of their cash.
"We do want to attract the customer into the store," Wozniak said. "We try our hardest."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Nisha Patel and Rukhsar Ali

articles.title: The corruption case against Benjamin Netanyahu just suffered a serious blow. What comes next?
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was handed a major legal victory this week when the judges in the years-long corruption trial against him suggested the prosecution reconsider one case, work…

image.caption: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to the media after voting at a polling station in Jerusalem in October. (Jewel Samad/AFPThe Associated Press)

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was handed a major legal victory this week when the judges in the years-long corruption trial against him suggested the prosecution reconsider one case, work out a plea deal in another and entirely drop the third — the most serious.

While the court clarified these were recommendations and not rulings, it was still a significant blow to the prosecution, which has sought to convict the prime minister on a series of charges related to allegations of bribery, fraud and breach of trust after he was indicted in 2019.
The prime minister has denied any wrongdoing, casting the charges as a witch hunt by hostile media, police and prosecutors.
But now, the future of the trial is in serious doubt as prosecutors decide how to proceed.
Here's a look at the cases, the charges, what the judges said and where it may go next.
Israeli judges call to drop 1 of Netanyahu's 3 corruption charges
What is Netanyahu charged with?
Netanyahu is facing charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases known as case 1000, case 2000 and case 4000.
On Wednesday, the judges overseeing the trial summoned Israel's Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to appear at the Jerusalem District Court.

"That never happens," Yael Friedman, the legal correspondent for the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, told CBC News. She has been covering the trial since it began in May 2020. "You just need to understand that it was a very irregular act."
Speaking for the court, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman proceeded to lay out their concerns or recommendations for each of the three cases.
Case 1000
Charges: fraud, breach of trust
In this case, Netanyahu is accused of accepting nearly $200,000 in gifts from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer.

Film producer Arnon Milchan leaves the Old Ship Hotel in Brighton, England, on on June 25, 2023, after giving testimony in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial. His testimony was transmitted via videolink to the District Court of Jerusalem. Prosecutors allege Milchan gave the Israeli prime minister expensive gifts in return for personal favours. (Chris Eades/Getty Images)
Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu lobbied on Milchan’s behalf on U.S. visa matters, tried to legislate a generous tax break for him and sought to promote his interests in the Israeli media market.
What the judges said: Work out a plea deal or settlement

“It seems to us that it is possible to get to a conclusion," Friedman-Feldman said, according to the Times of Israel. "We are open to all possibilities — we need to find the procedural way to get there."

Friedman told CBC News that she believes the court was suggesting that though there could be a conviction, the two sides should instead get together to come up with some kind of plea arrangement to finish the trial.
Case 2000
This case centres around two audio recordings of conversations between Netanyahu and Arnon Mozes in 2014.
Mozes is the the publisher of Yedioth Ahronoth, one of Israel's largest newspapers and Ynet, one of the largest news websites.

Arnon Mozes, left, the owner and publisher of Yedioth Ahronoth, one of Israel's leading newspapers, is seen in Lod, Israel, in January 2017. At right, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at the White House in January 2020, as U.S. casino magnate Sheldon Adelson looks on. (Reuters, Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Netanyahu was accused of offering to put forward legislation that would have helped restrict the circulation of the free daily newspaper Israel Hayom, also known as Israel Today, which is the main rival to Mozes' paper.
The irony is that Israel Hayom (Israel Today) is owned by the family of Sheldon Adelson, the late U.S. billionaire and casino magnate, who was also a supporter of Netanyahu.
Mozes has denied any wrongdoing.
What the judges said: Reconsider
The judges recommended prosecutors reconsider case 2000.
"Legally, this is a very, very problematic, case," said Moshe Cohen-Eliya, law professor and former president of the Tel Aviv-based College of Law and Business.

"What the court actually said is that basically there is no legal offence," Cohen-Eliya said in an interview with CBC News. "Maybe you have very good evidence about these kinds of negotiation between Netanyahu and Mozes. However there is no offence."
According to Friedman, the judge said that while she doesn't see the court convicting Netanyahu on case 2000, she gave the prosecution a chance to explain the charges.
"They're leaving it a bit open," Friedman said.
Case 4000
Charges: bribery, fraud, breach of trust
This was considered the most serious of the three cases as it includes the charge of bribery.

Netanyahu, while serving as both primer minister and communications minister from 2014 to 2017, was accused of seeking to ease regulations that would have benefitted Shaul Elovitch, then the controlling shareholder in Bezeq, Israel's largest telecommunications company.

Israeli businessman Shaul Elovitch appears in the Justice Court in Tel Aviv in one of the graft probes threatening Netanyahu on Feb. 22, 2018. Elovitch is accused of having given Netanyahu positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefiting his telecommunications business. (Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images)
In return, it's alleged that the news website Walla, owned by Elovitch at the time, would provide positive coverage of Netanyahu and his family.
The regulatory favours would be worth around ⁠1.8 billion shekels (about $500 million US) to Bezeq.
Elovitch has denied any wrongdoing.
What the judges said: Consider dropping the charges

As for case 4000, in relation to the bribery charge, Friedman-Feldman said there was "serious doubt as to whether the evidentiary basis supports this claim." The Times of Israel reported that she said "the chances of conviction are low" for all three charges.

This wasn't the first time the judges have raised concerns about the ability to prove the bribery charge. In May 2023, judges said prosecutors should consider withdrawing the charge, but the prosecutors declined to do so.

"So, from that perspective, it was already kind of like known that [the bribery charge] was the more weaker charge," Friedman said. "But what was surprising was how they basically overruled the whole 4000 case."
Has Netanyahu testified?
Netanyahu has testified in 98 hearings in 18 months of the trial, while Israel was at war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

"It was quite crazy, the situation where he gets, like, this note from one of his secretaries saying he needs to take an urgent call," Friedman said. "And he goes up to the judges and says, 'Um, excuse me, I need to take a break.' "

She says Netanyahu's testimony, which included many breaks within the 18 month time span, is the longest in Israel's history of criminal trials, and also notes that Netanyahu would show up for the testimony of major witnesses.
On Wednesday, the judges overseeing the trial summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to appear at the Jerusalem District Court. (Gil Cohen-Magen/The Associated Press)
What will the prosecution do?
The prosecution said it will take time to review the recommendations of the court. But Cohen-Eliya said he believes the attorney general will ignore the judges and continue with the trial.
"I can guess that she would go back to the court, and she would say, 'I heard you, but I'm still pursuing the case,' " he said.
Cohen-Eliya says the corruption case against Netanyahu is the most important one in Israel's history besides the trial of Nazi Adolf Eichmann in the 1960s.
"It's a lot at stake for the prosecution," he said.

Friedman says if the prosecutors "believe in the case and think that the judges are wrong" they could continue with the trial, get a verdict — even one that goes against them — and then appeal to the Israeli Supreme Court.
Another option, she says, is to start negotiating a plea deal.
"And then it depends how much they would want to compromise. And what would Netanyahu agree [to] compromise from his side?"

articles.title: This Independent is giving Poilievre's Conservatives the jitters ahead of a crucial byelection
articles.summary: The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is…

image.caption: Independent candidate Dave Carrol is running in the upcoming federal byelection in Brantford-Brant South. A local pastor, Carrol was running for the Conservative nomination but was snubbed by the party brass. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)

blocks.text: The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is trying to stop Tory rule in an upcoming byelection — and there are early signs he's gaining traction.
That candidate is Dave Carrol, a pastor at Freedom House — a big church with a long list of parishioners — and a local media personality with regular segments on Rogers TV.

Those positions, plus his decades of advocacy on issues like homelessness, and his "Captain Kindness" superhero persona at community events like the Santa Claus parade, have made him a known quantity in this mid-sized industrial city in Ontario's southwest.
With endorsements from past Conservative MPs in the area, including Phil McColeman and the outgoing Larry Brock, Carrol sought the party's nomination for the Dec. 7 vote.

items: Highest MP turnover rate in decades making for byelection bonanza this Parliament

blocks.text: But he never had the chance to test his support among the party faithful. Poilievre unilaterally appointed ex-mayor Kevin Davis as the candidate, upsetting Carrol and his supporters who thought he was best placed to keep the seat for the blue team. The party has since revoked his membership.
After being snubbed, Carrol struck out on his own, cobbling together the campaign team and resources needed to take on the Liberal-Conservative duopoly in this area.
If the election sign war is any indication, Carrol is poised to do better than most independents who vie for a seat in the House of Commons.
Parts of the city are blanketed with Carrol signs emblazoned with his campaign slogan: "People first. Community always."
In some neighbourhoods, the Carrol signs easily outnumber the Conservative ones.

If the election sign war is any indication, Dave Carrol is poised to do better than most independents who vie for a seat in the House of Commons. Parts of Brantford are blanketed with Carrol signs. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)
In an interview with CBC News, one of his first with a national news organization since his Conservative candidacy went awry, Carrol said this campaign is not about getting even with Poilievre.

"I've spent most of my adult life dressed up in a Captain Kindness costume, walking around talking about how to use kindness to transform a community. What I'm doing has absolutely nothing to do with revenge," he said.
But he said the party's move to block his candidacy and usurp the will of some local Conservative members did inspire him to jump into the fray.
'Not a revenge vote'
"We are frustrated with this decline in democracy," Carrol said.
"But this has not been a personal endeavour. This is not a revenge vote. This is not a protest vote. This is a purposeful choice to put people's voices at the forefront."
And so far, he said, the reception has been "tremendous," as his message of tackling the scourge of homelessness and addiction has resonated in a part of the province hit hard by both.
Still, he's cognizant of what a victory could mean for Poilievre and the Conservatives.
"There's a national spotlight because this is a consequential election," he said. "The people I talk to are not nervous, they're excited."
Brantford campaign has 'absolutely nothing to do with revenge,' Independent candidate says
But some federal Conservatives are feeling skittish.

This particular byelection has the potential to be hugely consequential for Poilievre given it's the one riding out of the six up for grabs that is most likely to change hands next month, according to a recent survey by Abacus Data. Brock won the seat by about 11 percentage points in the last federal election but Conservative support nationally has fallen off since then.
Poilievre has been a frequent presence in the riding this fall, often giving up his weekends to door-knock in a seat that could decide his fate.

There have been six federal byelections so far this year and the Conservatives have lost them all. Party sources told CBC News that if the Conservatives fall short in Brantford, it could ignite a movement to oust Poilievre as leader as some MPs grow restless after a prolonged losing streak.

One Conservative source described Brantford as Poilievre's "Toronto-St. Paul's moment," a reference to the 2024 Liberal byelection loss in a party stronghold that was the beginning of the end for former prime minister Justin Trudeau.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is seen on Parliament Hill on Thursday. Poilievre has been been in Brantford often in the lead up to the December byelection. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill this week, Conservative MP Ben Lobb said this election could be a nail-biter.
"I don't think anybody knows how that is actually going to go," Lobb said. "I think everybody would say it's close. So really, on that one, it's whoever gets out the vote."
Poilievre, meanwhile, has bristled at questions about what this Brantford byelection could mean for his tenure at the top.
"You all ask this question again and again and again over the last several days," Poilievre said at a news conference this week.

"I think we actually have to focus in the byelections on the simple questions: Can you afford your groceries more today than when Mark Carney became prime minister? Or is it time to lower costs with a Conservative approach?" he said.

items: Defence minister 'very concerned' after Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened

blocks.text: While Liberal candidate Joy O'Donnell, a local businessperson, is a serious contender for the seat given the party's recent strength in national polls, the Conservatives have so far focused their negative campaign messaging on Carrol.
In some homes across Brantford, voters have received direct mail from the Conservatives with a warning of what they say could happen: "A vote for Dave Carrol is a vote for the Liberals."
Carrol said he's not splitting the Conservative vote, claiming he's drawing support from voters of all political stripes who are tired of a party-dominated, "Ottawa knows best" approach.
"We have people who have not just voted for, but served across the political spectrum," he said.

Carrol is seen in his 'campaign cottage' in Brantford. Without access to sophisticated party databases, his campaign is relying on a team of dedicated volunteers to help him do what's not often done in Canadian politics: win as an Independent. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)
Carrol's Conservative opponent, was not available for an interview.
"As he approaches the final stretch of the campaign, Kevin is prioritizing his time at the doors, connecting directly with voters," a party spokesperson said of Davis.
Carrol doesn't have access to the sophisticated voter databases used by the big parties to track supporters and turn them out.

items: How to vote in the upcoming federal byelection for Brantford—Brant South

blocks.text: But there's a steady stream of campaign volunteers through Carrol's quaint office that he's taken to calling his "campaign cottage," given its rustic nature compared to the relatively more comfortable digs of Davis's strip mall election outpost just a few blocks away.
The campaign is doing things the old-fashioned way, sending its committed roster of volunteers out with a map and a clipboard to collect the names and phone numbers of potential Carrol supporters.
Independent Brantford byelection candidate disputes vote splitting after Conservative snubbing

While it's always an uphill battle as an Independent, Carrol said voters in this part of the Ontario heartland have a recent history of eschewing party politics and backing an independent candidate with deep roots in the community.

Ontario MPP Bobbi Ann Brady from the neighbouring Haldimand-Norfolk riding has a similar story. A longtime community advocate, she was passed over for the PC nomination when the party appointed a candidate and then ran as an Independent. Brady has since won the seat twice, with huge margins.
"I am fired up because I genuinely care about this. For me, this is not about politics. It's about people," Carrol said.
"And so do I think we have a chance of winning this? I absolutely do."

articles.title: Man in AI deepfake case admits to stalking women, voyeurism and more
articles.summary: One of two men accused in an AI deepfake case involving 45 alleged victims in Canada and the U.S. — including real-life victims of sexual violence and kidnapping — has pleaded guilty for the role he…

image.caption: Gregry Peter Joseph Van Beek faced seven charges prior to his guilty plea earlier this week, including harassment by watching and besetting, conspiracy to commit an indictable offence and publishing intimate images without consent. (Submitted/Name withheld)

blocks.text: WARNING: This story includes mentions of sexual violence and exploitation, including voyeurism, kidnapping and rape.

One of two men accused in an ongoing multi-jurisdictional investigation into violent and sexual AI deepfake images involving 45 alleged victims in Canada and the U.S. — including real-life victims of sexual violence and kidnapping — has pleaded guilty for the role he played.
Gregry Peter Joseph Van Beek (Vanbeek in court records) is a 39-year-old from West Nipissing, Ont., near Sudbury who often goes by Peter.

He sat in the prisoner's box of an Ottawa courtroom Monday afternoon and admitted to stalking three women in the capital, finding out where they lived and/or worked, taking photographs of two of them through a window, and obtaining photos and videos of others.
Van Beek also published intimate images of two women, made an online threat to rape one of them, and more.
Having these [pictures] is just another way to use her body without consent.Gregry 'Peter' Van Beek

In the commission of his crimes, Van Beek used a now-defunct pornography website called Motherless and the encrypted messaging app Session to communicate with the other man accused in the case, Stephen Lowe. Lowe is a Nova Scotian who is co-operating with police, according to assistant Crown attorney Matthew Brown, who is handling the case with fellow prosecutor Polina Leonov.
Other case moving through court

Lowe is facing 81 charges and remains before the court. He is alleged to have routinely shared biographical data about women with people using Motherless and Session, and invited the users to find and rape them, Brown told the judge in Van Beek's case on Monday.

Two of the stalking victims in Van Beek's case were referred by Lowe, Brown said and records show. Lowe shared with him that two young women were looking for an apartment in Ottawa, "so we know where she'll be as far as city goes, soon."
"F--k that's hot," Van Beek replied. "I'd love to stalk her again."
A message from Van Beek to Lowe, filed in court as evidence. (Ontario Court of Justice exhibit)
Lowe is also alleged to have uploaded 6,889 pieces of media to Motherless, which were viewed more than 1.5 million times, Brown said.

The charges against Lowe include 28 counts of criminal harassment, 26 counts of uttering threats to cause bodily harm, 24 counts of making and publishing obscene materials, and three counts of possessing, making and distributing child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
The allegations against Lowe have not been proven. His next court appearance is scheduled in December.
Images of unidentified girls shared
The facts against Van Beek came from Lowe's devices and website records handed over to police in response to production orders.
On Monday, Van Beek pleaded guilty to criminal harassment by watching and besetting, publishing intimate images of two women without their consent, and uttering a threat to cause bodily harm.

items: How police tracked down suspects in AI deepfake investigation involving dozens of women
Her husband is accused in an AI deepfake investigation. She’s filing for divorce
AI deepfake investigation by Ottawa police not trauma-informed, alleged victims say

blocks.text: Other agreed facts read out by the Crown included that Van Beek talked about personally recording women without their consent. He admitted going to a mall in Ottawa to "shoot creepshots" between 2009 and 2014, and admitted to finding girls at West Nipissing high schools and finding their friends on social media, Brown told court.

He sent 12 photographs of an unidentified teenage girl taken in a grocery store, as well as photos of her in a bathing suit taken from her social media, Brown said. Van Beek also sent 16 photos of another unidentified teenage girl at a hotel, and wrote that she caught him looking at her a few times and "looked uncomfortable."
'Fun' to focus on 'real life victims'
Van Beek and Lowe also wrote about wanting to rape victims of serial killers, kidnappings, rape and suicide, Brown said. Van Beek wrote that "it's fun" to fantasize about "real life victims."
The woman depicted in one of the intimate images Van Beek published is one such real-life victim of kidnapping and sexual violence.
Details about what happened to her, and her life since, cannot be published because they could identify her and breach a routine court-ordered publication ban that protects victims.

Van Beek found more than 50 "boudoir" photographs of her in lingerie with some nudity. He explained to Lowe that for years, he's browsed online services used by professional photographers to upload and house images to send to their clients, and found instances where photographers hadn't adequately privatized them.
2 charged over violent, sexual AI deepfakes of dozens of Canadian women

"Anyway I've collected hundreds, women from all walks of life, wives, nurses, teachers etc. ... some have been somewhat famous like news women, wives of major athletes or social media influencers," he explained to Lowe. "Long story short it's not like they are meant to be public but you can find them with some work. I've done that for years and am in some private online groups where I trade finds with others."
"Lucky would be the guy who kidnapped and raped her now!" Lowe wrote.
"Having these is just another way to use her body without consent," Van Beek replied.

Police spoke to Van Beek's wife during the investigation, Brown told court. She told them Van Beek had admitted to her back in 2017 that he was interested in voyeurism, and that she thought it had stopped.
'Underground fantasy behaviours'
Van Beek's defence lawyer James Foord stood in front of the judge after the Crown finished speaking and said the facts against his client were accurate, but he wished to comment.

His client, who has no criminal record and had never been in trouble with the law before, had "no knowledge" of any deepfake pornography images allegedly created by Lowe. "That was Mr. Lowe," Foord said.
In messages between Lowe and Van Beek filed in court, Van Beek told Lowe he had seen Lowe's AI content. It's unclear what content he had seen specifically.

Van Beek was involved in "underground fantasy behaviours," Foord said. And "one of the difficulties" in Van Beek's case is that the things he said online didn't always reflect what he did or what he was going to do, Foord added.
"It wasn't entirely masturbatory fantasy," Ontario Court Justice David Berg countered.
"It almost entirely was," Foord replied.
Van Beek and his wife attended couples therapy together after he admitted to voyeurism. Van Beek also sought individual therapy for his voyeurism addiction and managed to quit, Foord added.
"Unfortunately," Van Beek later returned to voyeurism, Foord said. Van Beek's wife continues to support him nonetheless, and Van Beek is committed to getting help, Foord concluded.
James Foord, seen here in 2019, is a criminal defence lawyer and past president of the Defence Counsel Association of Ottawa. (Laura Osman/CBC)
'There's a lot of context': Van Beek
The judge turned his attention to Van Beek and asked if he agreed to the lengthy facts read out by the Crown. Van Beek hesitated and looked at his lawyer.
As Berg began to ask Van Beek to look at him instead, Van Beek replied, "Yeah. Yes.... There's a lot of context, but yes."
"But the criminal behaviours that are described in here," Berg began to say.
"Yes," Van Beek said. "The four counts, yes."
Regardless of Monday's plea, the investigation into Van Beek continues. Court heard that police are still trying to unlock all the electronic devices seized from Van Beek when he was arrested in May.
If police do gain access to Van Beek's devices, it's possible more charges could be laid.
A sentencing hearing will take place in the new year. In the meantime, a sexual behaviours assessment has been ordered for Van Beek while he remains in jail.
Sexual violence resources
If you're in immediate danger, call 911.
For support in your area, you can find crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada, which maintains a database for every province and territory.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
articles.summary: The announcement comes a year after a military coup with its leaders promising a return to civilian rule within 12 months.

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte: We will accept whatever impeachment verdict
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President is ready to accept whatever verdict the Senate impeachment court issues, Vice President Sara Duterte said in a press conference.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 4:53pm

Vice President Sara Duterte chats with Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto as she attends the Senate deliberations on the Office of the Vice President’s budget for 2027 on November 26, 2026.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Vice President is ready to accept whatever verdict the Senate impeachment court issues, Vice President Sara Duterte said in a press conference on Friday, November 27.
Duterte told reporters that her office is “prepared for the worst,” saying that the OVP has discussed how to address the consequences that could come with a guilty verdict.
She said that the office’s primary concern is the loss of employment among staff whose tenure depends on Duterte’s position.
The OVP estimates that Duterte’s removal from office would result in the termination of these employees, affecting around 300 families nationwide.

The office has also discussed relocating to a different physical space, as its current address in Mandaluyong City was selected because it served as Duterte’s campaign headquarters during the 2022 elections.
Duterte also cited the possibility of public backlash over her removal, saying that voters could take issue with replacing an elected official with an appointee.
If Duterte is impeached, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. would have to nominate someone from Congress to fill her position.
Malacañang earlier said that Marcos has not decided on the vice president’s replacement.

An acquittal, meanwhile, would have little impact on the office’s operations, Duterte said, as it would allow the OVP to continue its current activities and focus on implementing its planned projects.
Duterte added that even in the event of an acquittal, her opposition would still have a year to launch another impeachment attempt or “do many other things” to her.

“By that time (a third impeachment case) siguro, mag-resign na ako kasi wala na talaga akong pambayad ng abogado … Puwede nila akong ipakulong. Puwede nila akong ipadala sa Pluto or sa ilalim ng lupa. Depende sa kanila.”

(By that time [a third impeachment case], I’ll probably resign because I don’t have money to pay for a lawyer anymore. They can have me imprisoned. They can have me sent to Pluto or buried underground. It depends on what they want.)
Asked if she would appear at the impeachment court to receive her verdict in person, Duterte said that she was still unsure, citing activities scheduled in Davao in December.
The vice president’s camp and members of the prosecution have both floated the possibility of the trial ending before the end of the year.
The Senate impeachment court has set hearings from December 1 to 4, with the vice president’s dentist and a Bureau of Customs official expected to take the witness stand.
The witnesses’ testimonies form part of Duterte’s defense against the second article of impeachment, which concerns her alleged unexplained wealth.
