articles.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
articles.summary:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local…
articles.byline: Amy Hawkins and Yu-chen Li in Taipei

blocks.text: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

blocks.caption: Cheng Li-wun travelled to China to meet Xi Jinping. Photograph: CTI/Reuters

blocks.text: Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

blocks.caption: Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

articles.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
articles.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.

blocks.text: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

articles.title: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.

blocks.text: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind

blocks.caption: Image caption, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.

items: Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat
Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties

blocks.text: Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months

blocks.text: Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

blocks.text: Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.

blocks.caption: Image caption, NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League

blocks.text: NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

blocks.text: Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

articles.title: Ombudsman orders graft raps vs 3 ex-Landbank officials, businessman
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the filing of graft charges against three former officials of the Land Bank of the Philippines and a private businessman over alleged irregularities in the…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 7:30am
Philstar.com / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the filing of graft charges against three former officials of the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) and a private businessman over alleged irregularities in the approval and renewal of loans extended to American Boulevard Trading Corp. (ABTC).

In a statement on Thursday, November 26, the Ombudsman said it found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction against former LBP First Vice President Lolita Silva, former Assistant Vice President Danilo Dayanghirang, former Account Officer Ronaldo Robles, and ABTC President and Chairman Alberto Ching for allegedly violating Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
The case stemmed from a complaint filed by LBP’s Loan Recovery Department following a February 2022 letter from then-Assistant House Majority Floor Leader Rowena Niña Taduran.
The letter flagged Ching’s disclosure that bank "insiders" had allegedly fast-tracked the approval and subsequent renewals of ABTC's loans in exchange for a 10% commission.

ABTC initially secured a P50-million short-term loan facility in August 2017, which was later increased to P100 million in February 2018 and eventually reached P115 million in September 2018, according to the Ombudsman.
According to the Ombudsman, an internal investigation and special audit conducted by LBP uncovered multiple violations of bank lending policies.

These included the diversion of loan proceeds for purposes other than those approved, the renewal of promissory notes despite existing past-due accounts, and the failure to properly assess the borrower’s financial condition and creditworthiness.

Investigators also found that the financial projections used to justify the loan approvals were significantly higher than historical figures, while material information regarding ABTC's financial obligations and outstanding loans was neither properly disclosed nor evaluated.

The Ombudsman also pointed out that Silva, Dayanghirang, and Robles, acting in conspiracy with Ching, allegedly disregarded established lending requirements and failed to exercise due diligence in facilitating the credit facilities.

“The investigation revealed that the respondents' actions gave unwarranted benefits, advantage, or preference to ABTC. The company also had outstanding loan obligations to LBP amounting to P141,305,054.24,” the Ombudsman said.

articles.summary: Sen. Erwin Tulfo interpolated during the hearing, citing the earlier hearing with the Department of Tourism, where accidents and drowning events at beaches caused by lacking safety signs were…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 7:00am
Sen. Panfilo "Ping" Lacson at the Senate budget hearing on the Department of the Interior and Local Government on Thursday, November 26.
YouTube / Senate of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government is seeking to add P176.89 million to their rescue and safety allocations to help local government units respond to tourist emergencies more efficiently.

During the budget hearing on Thursday, November 26, Sen. Erwin Tulfo asked if local government units had dedicated task forces to ensure the safety of tourist, especially in beaches, falls and other bodies of water.
Tulfo cited the earlier budget hearing with the Department of Tourism, where accidents and drowning events at beaches caused by lacking safety signs were discussed.
Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson answered that police are stationed in major tourist stations, but local government units also employ rescue personnel.
These personnel have completed their safety training, and the P176.89 million requested will complement existing funds, Lacson said.

Various water-related accidents have been reported in tourist spots around the country throughout the year. In November 2026, five tourists were rescued after being caught in a rip current while swimming in Baler, Aurora.
The DILG also led the high-profile investigation into the deaths of Ateneo de Manila University basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili.

The department’s Criminal Investigation and Detection Group recommended filing charges for violation of the Anti-Hazing Act against former Ateneo men’s basketball coach Tab Baldwin and 10 members of his coaching staff.

articles.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
articles.byline: Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short
articles.summary: Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in…
articles.byline: Roshni Majumdar, Sertac Comak, Kieran Burke

image.caption: Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 27, 2026
Antonia Costa wraps up EU summit that fails to close gaps in budget disputes

blocks.caption: Antonio Costa has a tough job to get EU members to agree on a common budgetImage: Marius Burgelman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.
That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.
Euro News reported earlier in the day that Bulgaria reversed course and was ready to join the loan, so long as it was only paying into the part that wasn't covering Ukraine's military needs.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was considerable work to be done before a deal could be in place.
EU leaders cut short a second day of talks that was due to take place tomorrow and pushed discussions to another summit in December.
The disagreements over a shared EU budget for the years between 2028 and 2034 stem from different priorities among EU members.
Some countries prefer greater funding for defense and enhancing competitiveness, while others seek to keep in place funding for agriculture, among other issues.
EU leaders ultimately weren't able to reach an agreement at the end of Thursday.

articles.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
articles.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search…

image.caption: Most of the "Flamingo Revolution" protests in Albania have been peaceful Image: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.
For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.
It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.
'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.
Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

blocks.caption: Clashes with police erupted in mid-October like here in TiranaImage: Adnan Beci/AFP

blocks.text: Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."
Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."
It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."
The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.
Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.
Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

blocks.caption: Albanians continue to call for the prime minister's resignationImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.
What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.
This article was translated from German.
Why Albania's political crisis is deepening

articles.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
articles.summary:
Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl…

blocks.text: In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects, raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

blocks.caption: Rani Gaidinliu has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.
The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

blocks.caption: Naga women photographing copies of Gaidinliu’s notebooks. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.
He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”
after newsletter promotion

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

blocks.caption: Gaidinliu was imprisoned in 1932 at the age of 17. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”
Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.
“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.
“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

articles.title: Cool ways to use solar panels on campus
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we get a university campus tour featuring some neat ways to use solar panels; see what's happening to old EV batteries instead of recycling; and find…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it's Bridget again. This week, I looked into creative solar panel designs and applications. The technology has come so far. Who knows, perhaps solar-panelled hats will become high fashion one day. I’d wear one.
This week:

items: Cool ways to use solar panels on campus
The Big Picture: A new job for old EV batteries
B.C. First Nation aims to be a model for wildfire prevention

blocks.text: Cool ways to use solar panels on campus

Joshua Pearce gives his students a tour of the solar panels on top of the Amit Chakma Engineering Building at Western University in London, Ont. (Free Appropriate Sustainability Technology (FAST) Lab at Western University)
A lot has changed since Joshua Pearce started in solar energy research more than 25 years ago.

“When I was a PhD student, you’d go to an energy conference and they’d almost laugh at you as a solar guy — like go back to your Lego blocks, we’re going to do ‘real energy’ with fossil fuels,” he said.
“Now, it’s the other way around, coal plants cannot compete with solar.”
Through technological advancements and the increased adoption of solar technologies, it is becoming much cheaper and easier to install solar panels, and create creative designs with them.
Pearce is now the Chair of Innovation at Western University in London, Ont., and solar is a booming industry in many parts of the world, though not necessarily in Canada.

And it’s not just huge solar arrays in fields. Pearce gave a photo tour of some of the interesting solar-powered installations at his university, from a picnic table to a mural. While they're only for demonstration and not commercially available, it's an interesting view of what's possible.
A picnic table with a plug
One of Pearce’s graduate students' first projects, a picnic table that can charge electronic devices. (FAST Lab at Western University)
This solar-powered picnic table is one of Pearce’s favourite applications.
It is made from recycled materials, including decommissioned panels from a solar farm and recycled plastic lumber, and creates enough power to charge laptops and cell phones.
The table sits in the engineering garden at Western University.
Cool designs now possible
One of Pearce’s students stands in front of a mural made of solar panels at Western University. (FAST Lab at Western University)
This angel wing mural is actually made up of solar panels.
“If you give up 10 to 20 per cent efficiency, you can make your solar panel look like whatever you want,” said Pearce.
“It can look like trees, the sky, bricks, your favourite cartoon character, dragons — whatever you want.”
That makes it possible to integrate solar panels as cladding, balcony railings, or coloured glass on windows — a growing trend called building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV).
Solar panels can come in a variety of colours now. (FAST Lab at Western University)
Solar panels can help increase agriculture yield
Solar panels can be installed either between rows of crops, or above crops that don’t need full sun exposure.

Pearce says that farmers can get more food out of the crops this way, compared to an open field, because the panels provide shade for crops that don’t need direct sunlight, or shelter from things like wind and hail.
He’s done experiments in Ontario which showed that, with solar panels set up, farms can get 18 per cent more strawberries, and almost double the number of pumpkins compared to normal farms.
Plus, sheep can graze under panels that provide shade, reducing the need to mow.
Other examples
Koami Hayibo, one of Pearce’s students, researches floating photovoltaic systems and their benefits. These solar panels are enough to power a house. (Submitted by Koami Soulemane Hayibo)
Other examples include solar fences, which Pearce says can be cheaper than wood fences in some instances, and can power things like pool water pumps.
Floating solar panels on water can also be beneficial because the water cools the panels, and the panels stop water from evaporating.
“We've looked at doing this in lakes that are going to die out if you don't conserve the water in some way, and that's a really great way to do it,” said Pearce.
He suggests that part of the lakes could be covered with floating panels, which can be done without disrupting fishing and swimming.
Pearce is excited about the future of solar energy — to help the environment, but also because in many cases, he says it’s becoming more cost-effective than using other building materials.
— Bridget Stringer-Holden

The Big Picture: A new job for old EV batteries
(Nick Nesbitt/Mapleview Energy)

The batteries in this photo once worked in a mine. They powered a special kind of EV — electric underground mining vehicles made by MacLean Engineering. But now they have a new job working at a farm in Elora, Ont.

The woman in the photo is Sandra Aragon Aviles, battery systems engineer at Mapleview Energy. The Ontario startup launched a pilot this summer that repurposed batteries from about four mining vehicles into a battery-and-solar system that has so far cut the farm's power costs by 37 per cent.

I met the company's founder and CEO Nick Nesbitt last week at the MaRS Climate Impact conference in Toronto. The timing was perfect, as I had been writing about what happens to EV batteries when they're no longer suitable for powering vehicles. Many EV battery recyclers have gone bankrupt. But more and more EV batteries are being repurposed as energy storage batteries at places like farms, factories and airports to save energy costs and provide emergency backup power. You can read more about this trend here.
— Emily Chung

blocks.text: B.C. First Nation aims to be model for wildfire prevention
Lori Daniels with the UBC Centre for Wildfire Coexistence, left, and Chief George Lampreau of the Simpcw First Nation in an area of forest being remedied. (Dave Dormer/CBC)
A First Nation in the B.C. Interior is hoping to be the model for wildfire resilience across the province.

The Simpcw First Nation, whose reserve is near Barriere, has partnered with the University of British Columbia's Centre for Wildfire Coexistence and the Co-Operators Resilience Acceleration Lab to form the Simpcw Wildfire Resilience Coalition.
The goal is to reduce the risk of wildfire around the community about 75 kilometres north of Kamloops.
The project involves a 1.5-square-kilometre cutblock, where crews have spent the last two years studying the land, then using heavy machinery to thin out trees and remove underbrush.
Around two-thirds of the trees and brush will be removed.
An area of forest prior to having trees and underbrush removed as part of the Simpcw Wildfire Resilience Coalition project. (Dave Dormer/CBC)
"If you look up the hills, you can see how thick the mountainside is, that's what we're reducing," said Simpcw Chief George Lampreau.
"Because if [a wildfire] gets into that, it'll spread across the top, and we're hopeful if it'll hit this, there's not enough trees to keep it going."
Lampreau added that planting trees is also part of wildfire mitigation.
"Instead of just coming back and planting some pine that'll grow fast, we're going to look at planting more of the birch, the aspen, so those ones will help contain the fires," he said.
The trees are processed and sold after removal in an effort to recoup some of the cost.
Lori Daniels, a co-director of UBC's Centre for Wildfire Coexistence, said that a goal of the project is to leave larger Douglas fir trees, which provide shade and are used by birds and animals.
Don Iveson is an executive adviser with Co-operators Resilience Accelleration Lab and says planning and paperwork for these types of projects can take years.
"One of the things we are working through with this project, is to understand where are the places where that permitting process can be more streamlined," he said.

"What advice can we give to the government of B.C. about making it easier for treatments like this to move ahead economically — so they can produce jobs, produce fibre supply, but also achieve risk-reduction in a timely fashion?"
If the project proves to be successful, Lampreau says he'd like to see the partnership model be used by other First Nations and communities around the province.
— Dave Dormer

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
articles.summary:
Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”
“The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16,” it added.
The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.
Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

blocks.caption: Palestinian children outside a residential block hit by Israeli strikes in Gaza City in 2025. Photograph: Ebrahim Hajjaj/Reuters

blocks.text: On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.
He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”
On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.

blocks.caption: Palestinians transport the body of Ahmed Abu Daher, 12, outside al-Aqsa hospital in central Gaza Strip. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire. Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head.
“I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day,” she added.
The Israel Defense Forces have been approached for comment.
Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.
A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.
According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians shelter in a destroyed school building in Khan Younis in 2024. Photograph: Hatem Khaled/Reuters

blocks.text: Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

articles.title: Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay
articles.summary: Despite delays due to health issues, the trial of the Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia has begun. Prosecutors say the defendant used her military contacts to provide information on German…

image.caption: The espionage suspect, whose face is pixelated, was seen in a Ukraine conference in Berlin in December 2025Image: Ukraine presidency

blocks.text: The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.
The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.
Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they said she would not confirm her personal information.
Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.
Espionage process with diplomatic fallout
The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.
The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.
Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.
Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.
The trial is expected to last until May 2027.
What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.
She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.
German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat
Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.
Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.
In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.
Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.
Russia rejects the allegations
The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.
Why Berlin remains an espionage hot spot
He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."
"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

articles.title: On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa
articles.summary: Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya: On his last trip to Africa, outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier called on companies at home to be bolder and seize opportunities in Africa.

image.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier (left) concluded his farewell tour to Africa with a visit to KenyaImage: Michael Kwena/DW

blocks.text: "My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was important to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," said Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.

"For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in the administration of former Chancellor Angela Merkel.
This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.
Germany is competing — not just with China
A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks."
As the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy company REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse.
"When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier also visited Anno's One Fine Day arts center in Nairobi Image: Rosalia Romaniec/DW

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.
This shows there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.

When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets.

The Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.
Vocational training meant to open up new prospects

But such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, 1 million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years.
Germany has said there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.
Is China shaping Africa's mobility future?

During his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.

There are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier said in Nairobi.
German SMEs also interested in Africa
Vocational training is said to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established.

"A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," said Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a company that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran."

"More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's new is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.

During the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he said, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses important raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," he said.
Opportunities for German automakers in Africa?
Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market.
"The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," said Audebert.
Germany's FM stresses Europe's 'need' for skilled workers

Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a new car," said Thill. This would mean that potentially 5-10 million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa.
Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," he said.
Not just business: African nations as political partners

Even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier said at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Kenya.
"These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," he said.

When asked to take stock of his 30 trips to African countries undertaken during his political career, Steinmeier said: "There is not one Africa, but many, and there are also very different, uneven developments there." This fact, he concluded, needs to be "communicated even more effectively" in Germany.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: KDgate for Montreal mayor continues with website mocking Kraft Dinner comments
articles.summary: Controversy in a box: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s Kraft Dinner comments spark website, impromptu protest at city hall.

image.caption: Boxes of Kraft Dinner were already visible near city hall on Thursday morning. (Simon-Marc Charron/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated
Controversy in a box: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s Kraft Dinner comments spark website, impromptu protest at city hall.
Soraya Martinez Ferrada acknowledged comment was awkward, but backlash continues
The controversy over her Kraft Dinner comments is sticking to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
The City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate – on Tuesday.
The budget is due to be adopted in mid-December.
But an ill-timed Kraft Dinner comparison over budget choices has been haunting the mayor, giving rise to a website created by a Montreal software developer presenting the city budget on KD boxes.
There is also a protest outside city hall later Thursday afternoon.
The landing page for the website, kdgate.ca, alludes to the mayor's comments. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

Martinez Ferrada’s comments during an interview with French-language media outlet Quartre95, a personal finance site, following the budget rollout compared creating a municipal budget to decisions taken at home.
"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.
"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because you can't afford filet mignon."
The comments were walked back by Martinez Ferrada on Wednesday morning in an Instagram story where she described the comparison as “clumsy.”
"What I meant was that when we make choices, the city is the same as when we make personal choices," she said.
The website, kdgate.ca, includes a rundown of the city budget listed in a way that mirrors the nutritional facts on the back of a food item. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)
But not before it unleashed a torrent of backlash on social media, framing her remarks as out of touch with the reality of Montrealers dealing with higher cost-of-living.
On Thursday morning, a website, kdgate.ca, was published outlining a municipal budget in the form of nutritional information on the packaging of the popular comfort food.

items: Montreal mayor walks back 'clumsy' Kraft Dinner comment after major tax hike
Montreal's 'unprecedented' tax hike key to tackling 'infrastructure crisis,' mayor says

blocks.text: Niko Draca, the Montrealer behind the site, told CBC News about what prompted him to create the site.
"I saw a lot of outrage over the comment and I wanted to turn it into something positive and really get people looking at this data," Draca said.
"These documents are usually quite long and dry, so I figured a fun way to visualize could help, basically using the KD comment as a hook."
Meanwhile, a “Soraya Dinner” is planned for Thursday afternoon in front of Montreal’s city hall.
Organizers are inviting demonstrators to bring a pot, a portable stove and their own ingredients.
Montrealers 'already at Kraft Dinner,' says Centraide CEO on mayor's post-budget comments
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sidhartha Banerjee is an assignment editor based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press and The Montreal Gazette. He can be reached at sidhartha.banerjee@cbc.ca.
